Interest Rates & Fixed Income Market.overview: This chapter builds the base for every interest rate derivative: how bonds and money market instruments are priced, how yields and prices move in opposite directions, and how duration and convexity measure that sensitivity. Revise the main Indian instruments (G-secs, T-bills, CDs, CPs, TREPS and repo), the shape of the yield curve, clean versus dirty price, and the relationship between coupon, current yield and yield to maturity. Practise small calculations such as zero-coupon pricing and duration-based price change, because they reappear in the hedging chapters.
questions: A zero-coupon bond with face value ₹100 matures in exactly 2 years. If the annual yield is 8% (annual compounding), what is its price?
Price = 100 / (1.08)^2 = 100 / 1.1664 = ₹85.73. ₹84.00 wrongly deducts simple interest of 16%, while ₹92.59 discounts for only one year.
An inverted yield curve means that:
Long-term yields are higher than short-term yields
Yields are the same for every maturity bucket
Corporate bond yields are below G-sec yields
Short-term yields are higher than long-term yields
An inverted curve slopes downward: short-tenor yields exceed long-tenor yields. It often signals expectations of falling rates or slower growth. A normal curve slopes upward.
Which money market instrument is issued by scheduled commercial banks to raise short-term funds?
Certificate of Deposit
Commercial Paper
Treasury Bill
Cash Management Bill

Certificates of Deposit are negotiable money market instruments issued by banks (and select financial institutions). Commercial Paper is issued by companies, while T-bills and Cash Management Bills are issued for the Government of India.
Which of these bonds will have the highest duration, assuming all yields are similar?
A 10-year bond paying a 9% coupon
A 5-year zero-coupon bond
A 10-year zero-coupon bond
A 10-year floating rate bond

A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, so the 10-year zero has duration of about 10 years. A coupon bond of the same maturity has lower duration, and a floating rate bond resets close to market, so its duration is very short.
The price a buyer actually pays for a bond bought between two coupon dates is the:
Clean price, i.e. the quoted screen price without any adjustment
Face value adjusted for the coupon rate
Clean price minus the accrued interest
Dirty price, i.e. clean price plus accrued interest

Bonds in India are quoted at clean price, but settlement happens at the dirty (full) price, which adds interest accrued since the last coupon date. The seller is thus paid for the interest earned while holding the bond.
In which money market segment do participants borrow and lend against government securities through a tri-party arrangement, with CCIL as the central counterparty?
TREPS
Call money market
Notice money market
Commercial paper market
TREPS (Tri-party Repo Dealing and Settlement) is a collateralised segment where CCIL acts as the tri-party agent and central counterparty. Call and notice money are uncollateralised interbank loans.
An 8% coupon bond is trading at ₹104 (face value ₹100). Which relationship among its yields is correct?
Coupon rate < current yield < YTM
Current yield < YTM < coupon rate
YTM < current yield < coupon rate
YTM = current yield = coupon rate
A bond priced at a premium has a current yield (8/104 = 7.69%) below its coupon, and its YTM is lower still because the ₹4 premium is lost by maturity. For discount bonds the order reverses.
A bond has a modified duration of 7 and convexity of 60. If its yield falls by 100 basis points, its approximate percentage price change is:
Change ≈ −MD × Δy + ½ × convexity × (Δy)² = −7 × (−0.01) + 0.5 × 60 × 0.0001 = 7% + 0.30% = +7.30%. Ignoring convexity gives 7.00%, which understates the gain.

Interest Rate Derivatives.overview: This chapter explains the main OTC and exchange-traded interest rate derivatives: forward rate agreements, interest rate swaps (including overnight indexed swaps), and bond and T-bill futures. Focus on how each contract is settled, who gains when rates rise or fall, and how futures are priced using cost of carry. For bond futures, understand the deliverable basket, conversion factor, basis and cheapest-to-deliver logic. Know that swap notionals are not exchanged and that a fairly priced swap has zero value at inception.
questions: In an overnight indexed swap (OIS), the floating leg payment is usually calculated by:
Using the 3-month term rate fixed once at the start of the reset period
Averaging the 10-year G-sec yield across the period
Compounding the daily overnight reference rate over the period
Taking only the overnight rate on the payment date

In an OIS the floating leg reflects the overnight rate compounded for every day of the reset period. In India the common benchmark is the overnight MIBOR, so the floating leg tracks actual daily funding costs.
A company has issued fixed-rate debentures but now expects interest rates to fall. Through an interest rate swap, it can benefit from falling rates by:
Receiving fixed and paying floating
Paying fixed and receiving floating
Paying fixed and receiving fixed
Buying a forward rate agreement

Receiving fixed offsets its fixed coupon outflow, leaving it effectively paying floating. If rates fall, its floating payments drop. Paying fixed would lock in the high cost, which suits a borrower fearing rising rates.
A '3×9 FRA' refers to an agreement covering:
A 9-month period starting 3 months from today
A 6-month period starting 3 months from today
A 3-month period starting 9 months from today
A 12-month period starting 3 months from today
FRA notation gives the start and end months from today. A 3×9 FRA starts in 3 months and ends in 9 months, so it fixes the rate for a 6-month period beginning three months ahead.
A deliverable bond's dirty price is ₹100. The repo (financing) rate is 6% p.a. and the bond earns coupon income at 7% p.a. Ignoring compounding, what is the theoretical 3-month futures price?
Futures = spot + financing cost − coupon income = 100 + (100 × 6% × 0.25) − (100 × 7% × 0.25) = 100 + 1.50 − 1.75 = ₹99.75. Because carry is positive, futures trade below spot.
In a plain vanilla rupee interest rate swap, what is exchanged between the parties at the start of the contract?
Nothing; the notional amount is not exchanged
The full notional amount, paid by each party to the other
The first year's interest paid in advance
A margin equal to 10% of the notional amount

The notional only serves to calculate interest payments. In a single-currency IRS it is never exchanged, and on each payment date only the net difference between fixed and floating interest changes hands.
At inception, the value of a fairly priced interest rate swap to each counterparty is:
Equal to the notional amount
Zero
Equal to one fixed-leg payment
Positive for the fixed payer only

The fixed rate in a fair swap is set so that the present value of the fixed leg equals the present value of the expected floating leg. Value arises later only as market rates move away from the contract rate.
Which of the following is NOT an interest rate derivative?
10-year G-sec futures
91-day T-bill futures
An overnight indexed swap
USD-INR currency futures
Currency futures derive value from an exchange rate, not an interest rate. G-sec futures, T-bill futures and OIS all derive their value from interest rates or interest-bearing instruments.
In bond futures, the 'gross basis' of a deliverable bond is defined as:
Futures price minus the bond's coupon rate
Conversion factor minus the bond's yield
Cash price minus (futures price × conversion factor)
Futures price multiplied by the accrued interest

Gross basis compares the bond's cash price with its adjusted futures price (futures × conversion factor). It reflects carry and the delivery option; the bond with the lowest net basis is usually the cheapest to deliver.

Exchange Traded Interest Rate Options.overview: This chapter covers options on interest rates and on bond prices or bond futures, along with caps, floors, collars and swaptions. The key idea is direction: bond-price calls gain when rates fall, while bond-price puts and interest rate caps gain when rates rise. Revise intrinsic and time value, break-even for buyers, the payoff of a caplet, and the net cost of a collar. Remember that option buyers pay a premium and have limited loss, while writers face larger risk and therefore post margins.
questions: A trader holds a put option on bond futures. The option gains value when interest rates:
Fall, because bond futures prices rise
Stay unchanged until expiry
Fall, because put premiums move with rates
Rise, because bond futures prices fall
Bond prices move opposite to yields. When rates rise, bond futures fall, so a put on bond futures moves into the money. A call on bond futures is the instrument that gains when rates fall.
A buyer pays a premium of ₹1.20 for a call option on a bond with a strike price of ₹100 (per ₹100 face value). Ignoring costs, the break-even price at expiry is:
A call buyer breaks even when the underlying price equals strike plus premium: 100 + 1.20 = ₹101.20. Below that the option does not recover its cost. ₹98.80 is the break-even for a put buyer.
A borrower's cap has a strike of 7% on a notional of ₹10 crore. For a quarterly period (0.25 year) the reference rate is set at 8%. The caplet payoff is:
Payoff = notional × (reference rate − cap rate) × period = ₹10 crore × 1% × 0.25 = ₹2,50,000. ₹10 lakh ignores the quarterly period fraction.
A put option on bond futures has a strike of 99.00 while the futures price is 97.50. Its intrinsic value is:
Put intrinsic value = strike − underlying price, if positive: 99.00 − 97.50 = 1.50. Any premium above 1.50 is time value. A call with the same strike would have zero intrinsic value.
Which of these options on bond futures has zero intrinsic value?
A call whose strike is below the futures price
A call whose strike is above the futures price
A put whose strike is above the futures price
A deep in-the-money put close to expiry
A call has intrinsic value only when the underlying price exceeds the strike. With the strike above the futures price the call is out of the money, so its whole premium is time value.
A 'payer swaption' gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to:
Enter into a swap receiving the fixed rate
Cancel an existing floating-rate loan
Enter into a swap paying the fixed rate
Buy a bond at a fixed future price

A swaption is an option on an interest rate swap. A payer swaption lets the buyer pay fixed (and receive floating), which is valuable if rates rise. A receiver swaption gives the right to receive fixed.
On exchange-traded interest rate options, margins are mainly collected from:
Option writers, since buyers pay the full premium upfront
Option buyers, since writers have already received the premium in cash
Both sides equally, as a fixed share of notional
Neither side, because options are fully pre-paid

A buyer's maximum loss is the premium already paid, so no further margin is needed. A writer's potential loss is large, so the clearing corporation collects margins from the seller to cover adverse moves.
A borrower buys a cap at 7.5% for a premium of 0.40% and sells a floor at 5.5% for a premium of 0.30% on the same notional. The net upfront cost of this collar is:
0.70% of notional
0.40% of notional
0.30% of notional
0.10% of notional
Net cost = premium paid − premium received = 0.40% − 0.30% = 0.10%. The floor income lowers the cost of protection, in exchange for giving up gains if rates fall below 5.5%.

Strategies Using Interest Rate Derivativ.overview: This chapter applies interest rate futures, swaps and options to real decisions: hedging bond portfolios, locking future borrowing or investment rates, changing portfolio duration, trading yield-curve views, and arbitraging mispriced futures. Learn the direction of each hedge (sell futures to protect against rising yields, buy to protect against falling yields), how to compute hedge ratios using duration or PVBP, and how to read profit and loss on a closed position. Curve trades (steepening and flattening) and calendar spreads are frequent scenario questions.
questions: You believe the gap between 10-year and 2-year G-sec yields will narrow because 10-year yields will drop more. Which futures position fits this view?
Buy long-tenor bond futures and sell short-tenor futures
Sell long-tenor bond futures and buy short-tenor futures
Sell both long-tenor and short-tenor futures equally
Buy only short-tenor futures and hold to expiry
If long yields fall relative to short yields, long-tenor futures will outperform. Buying them and selling short-tenor futures profits from the flattening while reducing exposure to a parallel shift.
A ₹25 crore bond portfolio has a modified duration of 4.8. A bond futures contract has a value of ₹2 lakh and a modified duration of 7.5. How many contracts are needed to fully hedge?
Contracts = (portfolio value × portfolio MD) / (contract value × futures MD) = (25,00,00,000 × 4.8) / (2,00,000 × 7.5) = 1,20,00,00,000 / 15,00,000 = 800 contracts, to be sold.
A fund manager wants to reduce the duration of a bond portfolio quickly without selling bonds. The manager should:
Buy interest rate futures
Buy call options on bond futures
Enter an IRS to receive fixed
Sell interest rate futures
Short futures have negative duration, so adding them lowers the portfolio's overall duration. Buying futures or receiving fixed in a swap would increase duration instead.
Bond futures are trading below their theoretical fair value. The reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage is to:
Sell the futures, buy the bond in the cash market and fund it via repo
Buy the futures, short-sell the bond and invest the proceeds
Buy both the futures and the bond at the same time
Sell the futures and hold cash until expiry

When futures are cheap, the arbitrageur buys futures and sells the bond in the cash market, investing the proceeds (reverse repo). At expiry the bond is received under the futures and returned, locking the mispricing.
A company plans to raise money by issuing bonds in two months and fears that yields will rise before then. Using interest rate futures, it should:
Buy futures now and sell them at issue
Wait and buy futures on the issue date
Sell futures now and buy them back at issue
Buy call options on bond futures now
If yields rise, the cost of borrowing rises but futures prices fall, so a short futures position gains and offsets the higher cost. Buying futures or calls would gain only if yields fell.
A bank sold bond futures to hedge its G-sec holdings. Yields then rise sharply. What is the most likely overall outcome?
Both the bond holdings and the short futures position make losses
Bonds gain while the short futures lose value
Short futures lose, doubling the bond losses
Loss on bonds is largely offset by a gain on short futures

Rising yields push bond prices down, causing a loss on the holdings. The same move lowers futures prices, so the short futures position gains. A well-sized hedge offsets most of the loss, leaving basis risk.
Simultaneously buying the near-month contract and selling the far-month contract of the same interest rate futures is called a:
Butterfly spread
Calendar spread
Basis trade
Straddle

A calendar spread uses two expiries of the same contract. Its margin is usually lower than for outright positions because most of the price risk offsets. A basis trade combines a cash bond with futures.
A trader sold 50 bond futures contracts (face value ₹2 lakh each, quoted per ₹100) at 99.20 and bought them back at 98.40. Ignoring costs, the result is:
Profit of ₹80,000
Profit of ₹8,000
Loss of ₹80,000
Profit of ₹8,00,000
Price fell by 0.80 per ₹100. Profit = 50 × 2,00,000 × 0.80 / 100 = ₹80,000. Being short, the trader gains when the price falls; ₹8,00,000 forgets to divide by 100.

Trading Mechanism.overview: This chapter explains how interest rate futures and options are traded on Indian exchanges: contract specifications, how prices are quoted, order types and their conditions, matching rules, client codes and the roles of trading and clearing members. Revise how T-bill futures are quoted, what happens to time priority when an order is modified, how open interest changes, and the difference between trading members and professional clearing members. Expect short scenario questions on order behaviour and open interest.
questions: On NSE, 91-day T-bill futures are quoted as:
The discount yield expressed directly in %
100 minus the annualised discount yield
The face value of the T-bill in rupees
The clean price of the T-bill per ₹1,000
T-bill futures are quoted as 100 minus the futures discount yield, so the quote rises when yields fall. This keeps the usual futures behaviour of price moving opposite to rates.
A sell stop-loss order on IRF with a trigger price of 98.50 becomes active when:
The market price rises to 98.50 or higher
The trading session ends at the closing bell
Open interest crosses a preset limit
The market price falls to 98.50 or lower
A sell stop-loss is used to cap losses on a long position. It stays inactive until the price drops to the trigger, at which point it is released as a limit or market order.
An order placed without any price limit that executes at the best price available in the order book is a:
Market order
Limit order
Stop-loss order
Good-till-cancelled order
A market order seeks immediate execution at the best available price. It offers certainty of execution but not of price. A limit order sets the worst acceptable price.
A trader changes the price of a pending limit order in the order book. What happens to its time priority?
It keeps its original time priority
It gets priority over all orders at that price
It loses its original time priority
It is automatically converted to a market order
Under price-time priority, a modification of price (or an increase in quantity) is treated as a fresh order and receives a new time stamp. This keeps the queue fair for orders already waiting.
Every client trading in exchange-traded IRDs must be identified on the trading system through a:
Demat account number of the trading member
Bank account number of the clearing member
Contract note number issued after trading
Unique Client Code linked to the client's PAN
Exchanges require every order to carry a Unique Client Code mapped to the client's KYC details, including PAN. This enables surveillance, position monitoring and correct allocation of trades.
A Professional Clearing Member (PCM) in the derivatives segment:
Clears and settles trades of trading members but does not trade
Trades on its own account and for clients but cannot clear any trades
Only provides price quotes as a market maker
Manages investor grievances for the exchange
A PCM is a clearing-only entity, typically a bank or custodian, that clears and settles trades executed by trading members tied up with it. It does not execute trades on the exchange.
Open interest in a futures contract represents:
The total number of contracts bought and sold during the whole trading day
The number of clients holding a demat account
The number of outstanding contracts not yet closed or settled
The total margin deposited with the clearing corporation
Open interest counts positions still open at the end of a period. Volume counts all trades in the period, including those that open and close positions on the same day.
Trader X opens a new long position of 10 contracts. The seller, Y, is closing out an existing long position of 10 contracts. What happens to open interest?
It rises by 10 contracts
It remains unchanged
It falls by 10 contracts
It rises by 20 contracts
One side opens and the other closes, so the open position simply passes from Y to X. Open interest rises only when both sides open new positions and falls when both sides close.

Clearing, Settlement & Risk Management.overview: This chapter explains how the clearing corporation guarantees exchange-traded interest rate derivative trades through novation, margins and default resources. Revise the types of margin (initial, extreme loss, calendar spread and mark-to-market), how daily MTM profit and loss is calculated, the role of clearing members and clearing banks, position limits, and the default waterfall including the Settlement Guarantee Fund. Understand cash settlement at expiry and practise simple MTM calculations using contract size and price quotes per ₹100.
questions: Initial margin on interest rate futures is generally computed using:
A flat 50% of the contract's notional value
The client's annual income declared in KYC
A portfolio-based risk model such as SPAN
The previous day's trading volume

Clearing corporations use portfolio-based models (SPAN-type methodology) that estimate the worst likely one-day loss across scenarios. The margin therefore reflects actual risk, with offsets for hedged positions.
A trader buys 10 IRF contracts (face value ₹2 lakh, quoted per ₹100) at 99.00. The day's settlement price is 99.40. The mark-to-market for the day is:
Gain of ₹8,000
Gain of ₹800
Loss of ₹8,000
Gain of ₹80,000
MTM = 10 × 2,00,000 × (99.40 − 99.00) / 100 = ₹8,000. As a buyer, the trader gains when the settlement price rises. It is credited in daily settlement.
A clearing member's main role in the derivatives segment is to:
Design and list new interest rate futures contracts for the exchange
Settle the obligations of trades executed by its trading members
Set the policy repo rate for the market
Issue government securities on behalf of RBI
Clearing members meet funds settlement obligations with the clearing corporation for trades of their own and of the trading members whose trades they clear, and they collect margins from them.
The Settlement Guarantee Fund (Core SGF) of a clearing corporation is used to:
Pay brokerage to trading members
Fund new product launches by the exchange
Compensate investors for market losses
Complete settlement when a member defaults
The Core SGF is a pool that ensures trades settle even if a clearing member fails to meet obligations. It is used after the defaulter's own margins and contributions in the default waterfall.
Why is margin on a calendar spread position usually lower than on two outright positions?
The long and short legs largely offset each other's risk
Spread positions cannot make any loss
Calendar spreads are not marked to market
Clearing corporations ignore far-month contracts
In a calendar spread the two legs move closely together, so the net risk is much smaller than that of two independent positions. Margin models recognise this with a lower spread charge.
For a cash-settled IRF, the final settlement price at expiry is derived from:
The last traded price of any equity index
Prices or yields of the underlying security in the cash market
The opening price of the contract on its first day
A price chosen by the client before expiry
Cash-settled contracts close by paying the difference between the trade price and a final settlement price, computed from prices or yields of the underlying G-sec or T-bill in the cash market.
Position limits on interest rate futures for clients and members are mainly meant to:
Guarantee a minimum daily profit to every participant in the contract
Fix the maximum brokerage a member can charge
Restrict trading to institutional investors only
Prevent excessive concentration and market manipulation
Position limits stop any single participant from building a dominant position that could distort prices or create settlement risk. They are a key part of the risk containment framework.
A client fails to pay the mark-to-market loss on IRF positions. Who remains liable to the clearing corporation for the settlement obligation?
The stock exchange on whose platform the trades were originally executed
SEBI, as the market regulator
The clearing member through whom the trades are cleared
The issuer of the underlying government security
The clearing corporation deals only with clearing members, who must meet obligations on time whether or not their clients pay. The member then recovers dues from the trading member or client.

Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter maps which authority regulates what in India's interest rate derivatives market. RBI frames the overall policy for rupee interest rate derivatives, including OTC products, user and market-maker categories and FPI limits, while SEBI regulates stock exchanges, clearing corporations and brokers on which exchange-traded IRDs are traded. Revise the key statutes (RBI Act, SCRA, SEBI Act), the suitability duties towards retail users, and SEBI regulations against fraudulent and unfair trade practices. Questions are usually conceptual rather than numeric.
questions: Stock exchanges and clearing corporations on which interest rate futures are traded are regulated by:
Reserve Bank of India
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Clearing Corporation of India Ltd
SEBI

SEBI regulates market infrastructure institutions such as stock exchanges and clearing corporations, including their exchange-traded interest rate derivative segments, while RBI sets the broader policy for IRDs.
RBI's power to regulate interest rate derivatives comes mainly from:
The Companies Act, 2013
Chapter III-D of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Depositories Act, 1996
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

Chapter III-D of the RBI Act gives RBI powers over interest rate derivatives, money market instruments and related transactions. RBI's Rupee Interest Rate Derivatives Directions are issued under these powers.
Under RBI's framework for OTC rupee IRDs, a corporate that enters into a swap with a bank purely to hedge its loan is classified as a:
Market-maker
Clearing member
User
Primary dealer
RBI divides participants into market-makers (who quote prices, such as banks and primary dealers) and users (who use derivatives to hedge or manage risk). A corporate hedging its loan is a user.
Before offering an OTC interest rate derivative to a retail user, a market-maker must:
Carry out a suitability and appropriateness assessment
Obtain prior written approval from SEBI for each individual transaction
Guarantee the user a minimum return
Ensure the user holds a demat account with CDSL

RBI requires market-makers to assess whether the product suits the retail user's needs and understanding, and to disclose risks clearly. This protects less sophisticated users from unsuitable products.
Spreading false information to move bond futures prices for personal gain would violate:
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations
SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations
The Foreign Exchange Management Act's current account rules
The Banking Regulation Act's licensing provisions
The PFUTP Regulations prohibit manipulative and deceptive practices in the securities market, including spreading misleading information to influence prices of exchange-traded derivatives.
An entity wishing to deal for clients in exchange-traded interest rate futures must be:
Licensed by RBI as a scheduled commercial bank with a treasury desk
Registered with IRDAI as a corporate agent
Registered with SEBI as a stock broker and be an exchange member
Approved by AMFI as a distributor
Trading members in the exchange IRD segment are stock brokers registered with SEBI and admitted as members of the exchange. Bank status or AMFI registration is not what permits trading for clients.
Investment limits for foreign portfolio investors in exchange-traded interest rate futures are prescribed by:
RBI
SEBI alone
The stock exchange board
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Because IRF positions relate to the government debt market and capital flows, RBI sets the limits for FPI participation. SEBI and exchanges then implement monitoring of those limits.
Under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, a contract for differences or an instrument deriving value from an underlying is treated as a:
Negotiable instrument
Deposit
Commodity
Security
The SCRA's definition of 'securities' includes derivatives. This is why exchange-traded derivatives, including interest rate futures, fall within SEBI's regulatory framework.

Accounting and Taxation.overview: This chapter covers how interest rate derivative positions are recorded in books of accounts and how profits are taxed. Revise the treatment of initial margin and option premium, recognition of mark-to-market gains and losses, the difference between fair value hedges and cash flow hedges under Ind AS 109, and the principle-based hedge-effectiveness test. On taxation, focus on why eligible exchange-traded derivative trades are treated as non-speculative business income, the documentation required, and how losses can be carried forward. Avoid memorising section numbers, which changed with the new Income-tax Act.
questions: Initial margin paid to the broker for an IRF position is best recorded in the books as:
An asset, being a deposit recoverable from the broker
An expense charged to profit and loss immediately
A liability payable to the clearing corporation
Part of share capital of the business
Initial margin is money placed with the broker or clearing member as security and is refundable when positions close, so it is shown as a current asset, not as an expense.
A bank hedges the change in fair value of its fixed-rate bond holdings by selling interest rate futures. Under Ind AS 109, this is a:
Cash flow hedge
Net investment hedge
Fair value hedge
Speculative position
A fair value hedge protects against changes in the value of a recognised asset or liability. Hedging the price of fixed-rate bonds against rate moves is a classic fair value hedge.
A company uses an IRS to fix the interest it will pay on a floating-rate loan. Under a cash flow hedge, the effective portion of the swap's fair value change is recognised in:
Retained earnings directly
Share premium account
Revenue from operations
Other comprehensive income
In a cash flow hedge, the effective part of the derivative's gain or loss is taken to OCI (cash flow hedge reserve) and later reclassified to profit or loss when the hedged interest affects earnings.
A business loss from eligible exchange-traded interest rate derivative trading, treated as non-speculative, can be carried forward for up to:
4 assessment years
8 assessment years
2 assessment years
Only the same year
Non-speculative business losses can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years and set off against business income. Speculative losses have a shorter carry-forward period.
For a derivative trade on a recognised exchange to be treated as non-speculative for tax purposes, it must be supported by:
An auditor's certificate issued for each trade
A bank statement showing a debit of the full notional
A time-stamped contract note with the client's unique code and PAN
A demat statement showing delivery of the bond

Tax law treats eligible derivative transactions on recognised exchanges as non-speculative only when they are carried out through a registered broker and supported by a time-stamped contract note showing unique client identity and PAN.
When a buyer pays premium for an interest rate option, the premium is initially recorded as:
Income in the profit and loss account
A reduction in the bank loan balance
Part of the borrower's equity reserve
An asset, until the option is exercised or expires
The premium buys a right, so it is carried as an asset (measured at fair value). It is adjusted on exercise, sale or expiry, with any loss reflected in profit or loss.
Under Ind AS 109, hedge effectiveness is assessed mainly by checking that:
Hedge results stay within a fixed 80%–125% offset range at every single reporting date
An economic relationship exists and the hedge ratio reflects actual risk management
The hedging instrument is always traded on an exchange
The hedge produces a profit in every reporting period

Ind AS 109 dropped the rigid 80–125% test of the older standard. Instead it requires an economic relationship, credit risk not dominating value changes, and a hedge ratio consistent with actual risk management.
A trader closes out an IRF position held for trading purposes. The cumulative gain on the position is recognised:
In profit and loss
Directly in share capital
As a contingent liability
Only when the trader files a tax return
Futures held for trading are measured at fair value through profit or loss, so gains and losses flow into the statement of profit and loss, both daily through MTM and on final close-out.

Code of Conduct & Investor Protection.overview: This chapter sets out the conduct expected from trading members who deal with clients in interest rate derivatives, and the protections available to investors. Revise KYC and risk disclosure duties, issue of contract notes, segregation and running-account settlement of client funds, prohibition on guaranteed returns and front-running, suitability for unsophisticated clients, and grievance and compensation routes such as SCORES, online dispute resolution and the exchange Investor Protection Fund. Most questions are scenario-based: identify the correct, ethical action for the broker.
questions: Before a client starts trading in exchange-traded derivatives, the trading member must provide the client with:
A guarantee that losses will be limited
The Risk Disclosure Document explaining derivative risks
A copy of the exchange's annual report
The trading member's own income tax return
Exchanges and SEBI require members to give clients a Risk Disclosure Document covering leverage, margin calls and possible losses, so the client understands derivative risks before trading.
A trading member must issue a contract note for executed trades to the client within:
7 working days of the trade
The end of the calendar month
The expiry date of the contract
24 hours of the trade
Contract notes, physical or electronic, must reach the client within 24 hours of execution. They record trade details and charges and serve as legal evidence of the transaction.
Running-account settlement of an active client's unused funds by the broker must be done:
Periodically, at least quarterly or monthly as the client opts
Only when the client finally closes the trading account with the broker
Once every two years after an audit
Only if the client files a written complaint
SEBI requires brokers to settle unused client funds on a periodic basis according to the client's choice of monthly or quarterly settlement, so client money does not stay idle with the broker.
A dealer tells a client, 'This IRF strategy cannot lose money; I guarantee 12% a year.' This is:
Acceptable if the client is a bank
Acceptable if given in writing
A violation of the code of conduct
Required to help the client decide
Brokers must not guarantee returns or make misleading statements about derivatives, which can always cause losses. Such assurances violate the SEBI code of conduct for stock brokers.
A dealer learns of a large client order to sell bond futures and first sells for the firm's own account. This practice is called:
Hedging
Arbitrage
Netting
Front-running
Trading ahead of a known client order to profit from its price impact is front-running. It misuses confidential client information and is prohibited.
The Investor Protection Fund (IPF) of a stock exchange is used mainly to:
Pay eligible claims of investors against a defaulting trading member
Make good the market losses suffered by investors on their open trading positions
Fund the exchange's advertising campaigns
Pay incentives to brokers with high volumes
When a trading member is declared a defaulter, the IPF compensates eligible investor claims up to set limits. It does not cover losses from adverse market movements.
A broker uses money lying in Client A's account to meet Client B's margin call. This is:
Permitted if both clients use the same branch
Permitted for up to three working days
Not permitted, as each client's funds must be used only for that client
Permitted when the broker is a clearing member
Client funds are held for that client's own obligations. Using one client's funds for another, or for the broker's own purposes, breaches SEBI rules on segregation and monitoring of client funds.
A retired client with no derivatives experience asks to take large leveraged IRF positions after hearing a tip. The broker's most appropriate step is to:
Execute the order immediately, since the client has clearly asked for it in writing
Explain the risks, assess suitability and record the advice given
Refuse to open any account for the client
Promise to reverse any losses within a week

Brokers should ensure the client understands leverage and margin calls, check whether the product fits the client's profile and keep records. Refusing outright or blindly executing are both poor practice.

Investment Landscape.overview: This chapter introduces why people invest and the choices available to them: physical versus financial assets, the risk-return trade-off, the main types of investment risk, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. It also covers asset allocation (strategic and tactical), the stages of an investor's life and wealth cycle, and common behavioural biases such as herding and loss aversion. Practise real-return and compounding calculations, and be able to identify which risks can and cannot be diversified away.
questions: A bank deposit earns 9% a year while inflation is 5%. Using the exact (Fisher) method, the real rate of return is closest to:
Real return = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.09 / 1.05 − 1 = 3.81%. Simply subtracting gives 4.00%, a rough approximation that slightly overstates the real return.
Which of the following is a financial asset?
Gold jewellery kept in a locker at home
Agricultural land held for farming
A commercial shop let out on rent
Units of a gold exchange traded fund
A gold ETF unit is a claim on a fund's assets, which makes it a financial asset even though the fund holds gold. Jewellery, land and property are real (physical) assets.
An investor buys a small cap fund only because colleagues and relatives have recently bought it. This behaviour is best described as:
Herd mentality
Anchoring
Loss aversion
Mental accounting
Herding means following what others do rather than independent analysis. Anchoring is over-reliance on a reference number, and loss aversion is feeling losses more than equivalent gains.
A planner temporarily raises equity from the long-term 60% to 70% because valuations look attractive, planning to return to 60% later. This is:
Strategic asset allocation
Rupee cost averaging
Tactical asset allocation
Portfolio rebalancing to target

Tactical allocation is a short-term deviation from the strategic mix to exploit market conditions. Strategic allocation is the long-term mix based on goals and risk profile, which the planner intends to restore.
A retired person drawing regular income from accumulated savings, with little new saving, is in which stage of the wealth cycle?
Accumulation stage
Transition stage
Inter-generational transfer stage
Distribution (reaping) stage
In the distribution stage the investor lives off the corpus built earlier. Accumulation is the earning-and-saving phase, and transition is the period just before retirement when goals come close.
Which risk cannot be reduced simply by adding more stocks to an equity portfolio, however many are added?
Market (systematic) risk
Company-specific risk
Management risk of one firm
Sector concentration risk

Systematic risk comes from factors like interest rates, inflation or recessions that affect the whole market, so diversification within equities cannot remove it. Company and sector risks fall as holdings are spread.
Which asset is generally the least liquid for an individual investor?
Units of a liquid fund
Shares of a large listed company
A residential flat
A savings bank deposit

Selling property takes time, involves negotiation, legal work and transaction costs, and may need a price cut. Liquid fund units, large-cap shares and savings deposits can be converted to cash within a day or two.
₹5,00,000 is invested at 8% a year, compounded annually. What will it be worth after 5 years (nearest rupee)?
Future value = 5,00,000 × (1.08)^5 = ₹7,34,664. ₹7,00,000 is simple interest for 5 years, while ₹7,93,437 is the compounded value after 6 years.

Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund.overview: This chapter explains what a mutual fund is, how it pools investor money, and the benefits and limitations of investing through one. It covers open-ended, closed-ended and interval schemes, and SEBI's categorisation of equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented and other schemes, including the investment rules that define each category. Revise distinctive features such as focused funds' stock limit, the value/contra choice, credit risk funds' rating rule and lock-ins for ELSS and solution-oriented schemes.
questions: An interval scheme is one that:
Allows purchase and redemption with the AMC on every single business day of the year
Never allows redemption until its final maturity
Allows purchase and redemption only during specified transaction periods
Pays interest to unitholders at fixed intervals
Interval schemes combine features of open and closed-ended schemes. Units can be bought or redeemed only during pre-announced intervals; at other times they are traded on a stock exchange.
A Fund of Funds (FoF) scheme primarily invests in:
Units of other mutual fund schemes
Shares of asset management companies
Bank fixed deposits of different tenors
Government securities only
An FoF builds its portfolio from units of other schemes, domestic or overseas. Investors get diversification across funds but bear an additional layer of expenses.
Under SEBI categorisation, a focused fund may hold a maximum of:
20 stocks
30 stocks
50 stocks
100 stocks
A focused fund invests in a concentrated portfolio of at most 30 stocks. It must state the market cap focus (large, mid, small or multi) and invest at least 65% in equity.
Under SEBI categorisation, an AMC may offer:
Both a value fund and a contra fund at any time
A contra fund only if it also runs a value fund
Neither, as these categories were withdrawn
Either a value fund or a contra fund, but not both
SEBI permits one scheme per category. Value and contra funds are treated as alternatives within one slot, so a fund house may offer only one of the two.
A credit risk fund must invest at least 65% of its assets in:
Corporate bonds rated AA and below, excluding AA+
AAA-rated public sector bonds only
Government securities of any maturity
Money market instruments maturing within 91 days
Credit risk funds seek extra yield by taking lower-rated paper: at least 65% in corporate bonds rated AA and below (excluding AA+). This raises both potential return and default risk.
Which is a limitation of investing through a mutual fund compared with holding shares directly?
The investor gets no professional management at all
The investor cannot tailor the portfolio to personal preferences
The investor cannot redeem units in an open-ended scheme
The investor must buy at least one full share of each company
A scheme follows its stated mandate for all investors, so individual choices on specific stocks cannot be accommodated. Professional management and liquidity are benefits, not limitations.
Retirement and children's funds (solution-oriented schemes) carry a lock-in of:
Exactly 3 years from the date of each individual investment
No lock-in, but an exit load of 1%
10 years for all investors
At least 5 years, or till retirement or majority if earlier
Solution-oriented schemes have a lock-in of at least 5 years or until the retirement age or the child attaining majority, whichever is earlier, to encourage goal-based investing.
A balanced advantage (dynamic asset allocation) fund differs from an aggressive hybrid fund mainly because it:
Must always hold between 65% and 80% of its assets in equity instruments
Invests only in government securities
Can vary its equity–debt mix dynamically within a wide range
Is a closed-ended scheme with fixed maturity
Balanced advantage funds shift between equity and debt (0–100%) based on a model or view. Aggressive hybrid funds must keep equity between 65% and 80% of assets.

Legal Structure of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter describes the three-tier structure of an Indian mutual fund: the sponsor who establishes it, the trust and trustees who protect unitholders, and the AMC that manages money. It also covers service providers such as custodians, RTAs and fund accountants, and the industry body AMFI. Revise sponsor eligibility, the trust deed, restrictions on AMC activities, trustees' reporting duties, the 'skin in the game' requirement, and the circumstances in which a scheme may be wound up.
questions: Under the traditional eligibility route, a sponsor must contribute at least what share of the AMC's net worth?
SEBI's traditional sponsor eligibility requires the sponsor to contribute at least 40% of the AMC's net worth, along with conditions on track record, profitability and net worth of the sponsor.
Which constituent calculates the NAV of a scheme by recording income, expenses and valuations?
Custodian
Fund accountant
Collecting banker
Trustee
Fund accounting, whether done in-house by the AMC or outsourced, records all transactions and computes the daily NAV. The custodian holds securities and the collecting bank receives investor money.
Which of the following activities is an AMC NOT permitted to undertake?
Managing portfolios under PMS through a separate business unit
Offering advisory services to pooled funds, subject to SEBI conditions
Acting as a trustee of any mutual fund
Managing its own schemes' investment portfolios

SEBI regulations bar an AMC from acting as trustee of any mutual fund. AMCs may undertake certain other permitted businesses, such as PMS or advisory services, with safeguards against conflicts of interest.
The document through which the sponsor creates the mutual fund as a trust is the:
Trust deed
Investment Management Agreement
Scheme Information Document
Memorandum of Association of the AMC

The sponsor executes a trust deed in favour of the trustees, which is registered under the Indian Registration Act. The Investment Management Agreement is a separate contract between trustees and the AMC.
CAMS and KFin Technologies are examples of which type of mutual fund service provider?
Custodians
Registrar and Transfer Agents
Credit rating agencies
Stock exchanges
RTAs process purchases, redemptions and switches, maintain unitholder records and send statements on behalf of AMCs. CAMS and KFin Technologies are the major RTAs in the Indian mutual fund industry.
SEBI requires AMCs to invest a minimum amount in their own schemes, linked to each scheme's risk level. The main purpose is to:
Provide the AMC with guaranteed income
Allow the AMC to vote on behalf of investors
Align the AMC's interests with those of unitholders
Increase the scheme's expense ratio
This 'skin in the game' rule means the AMC shares in the scheme's outcomes, which encourages responsible management. Higher-risk schemes require larger minimum investments by the AMC.
A scheme can be wound up if unitholders pass a resolution to that effect. What majority is required?
Three-fourths (75%) of the unitholders
A simple majority of more than 50%
Two-thirds of the trustees only
Ninety per cent of the AMC's directors
Regulations allow a scheme to be wound up if 75% of its unitholders pass a resolution, or when the trustees decide so for stated reasons, or when SEBI directs it in the interest of unitholders.
Trustees of a mutual fund are required to submit reports on the fund's activities to SEBI:
Only when a scheme is wound up
Every five years
Only if an investor complains
Every half-year
Trustees must file half-yearly reports with SEBI on the activities of the mutual fund, confirming compliance by the AMC. This is part of their supervisory role over the AMC.

Legal and Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers the rules that govern how mutual funds invest, advertise and treat investors. Revise SEBI's investment restrictions (single-issuer limits, ownership limits in a company, borrowing limits), advertisement rules and standard warnings, treatment of unclaimed amounts, and the duties placed on distributors under the AMFI code of conduct and SEBI norms such as commission disclosure. Also know the source of SEBI's powers and how investor complaints move from the AMC to SCORES and then online dispute resolution.
questions: Excluding index and sector-specific schemes, a mutual fund scheme cannot invest more than what share of its NAV in the equity shares of a single company?
SEBI caps investment in equity of any one company at 10% of a scheme's NAV, to ensure diversification. Index funds and ETFs may follow index weights, and sectoral funds have separate treatment.
All schemes of a mutual fund taken together cannot own more than what share of any company's paid-up capital carrying voting rights?
The 10% fund-house-level limit on voting capital prevents a mutual fund from gaining control or undue influence over a company it invests in.
A mutual fund may borrow money:
Freely and for any tenure, to increase the scheme's exposure to equity markets beyond its net assets
Only from its sponsor, without any limit or tenure
Never, as borrowing of any kind is fully prohibited
Only for temporary liquidity needs, up to 20% of net assets for 6 months

Borrowing is allowed only for temporary liquidity needs, such as redemptions or IDCW payouts, and is capped at 20% of net assets for a maximum of six months. Leveraging to buy securities is not permitted.
Which statement about mutual fund advertisements is correct?
They may promise a minimum return for equity schemes if the AMC has a long and consistent track record
They must carry the standard risk warning and show performance against the benchmark
They may use performance of only the best year
They do not need any disclosure if shown online

SEBI's advertisement code requires the standard warning about market risks and, where performance is shown, comparison with the benchmark over standard periods. Selective or assured-return claims are not allowed.
Unclaimed redemption and IDCW amounts lying with a mutual fund are:
Transferred to the AMC's own profit and loss account after one full year of remaining unclaimed
Kept idle in a current account without any return
Invested in special plans of liquid or money market schemes
Distributed among the other unitholders of the scheme
SEBI requires unclaimed amounts to be invested in specially created plans of liquid, overnight or money market schemes, so they keep earning returns until claimed by the rightful investors.
SEBI derives its statutory powers to regulate mutual funds primarily from the:
Companies Act, 2013
Indian Trusts Act, 1882
Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
SEBI Act, 1992
The SEBI Act, 1992 established SEBI and gave it powers to regulate collective investment vehicles including mutual funds. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 are framed under this Act.
A distributor tells a client that a credit risk debt fund is 'as safe as a bank fixed deposit'. This is:
Acceptable if the fund has never defaulted
A misrepresentation that breaches the code of conduct
Acceptable because both are debt products
Required to simplify things for the investor
Mutual fund schemes are market-linked and carry credit and interest rate risk; they carry no deposit insurance. Comparing a credit risk fund to an FD misleads the investor about risk.
When recommending schemes, a mutual fund distributor is required to disclose to the investor:
The commissions it receives from the AMCs for the schemes recommended
Its personal income tax returns and bank statements for the last three financial years
The fund manager's salary details
A guarantee of the scheme's future performance
SEBI requires distributors to disclose all commissions, such as trail payments, received from competing schemes they recommend. This helps investors see any conflicts of interest.

Scheme Related Information.overview: This chapter covers the documents and disclosures that tell investors about a scheme: the Scheme Information Document, Statement of Additional Information, Key Information Memorandum, Scheme Summary Document, addenda and annual reports. It also explains product labelling with the riskometer, the Potential Risk Class matrix for debt schemes, and fundamental attributes whose change triggers an exit option. Revise which document contains what information, the six riskometer levels, and the frequency of portfolio disclosures for different scheme types.
questions: Product labelling of a mutual fund scheme mainly informs the investor about:
The fund manager's personal investment record and qualifications over the last ten years
The scheme's nature and its risk level on the riskometer
The guaranteed return for the next year
The commission structure for distributors
Product labels describe the scheme's objective and type of investment in simple words and show a riskometer, helping investors judge whether the scheme suits them.
Which of the following is NOT one of the six levels on SEBI's mutual fund riskometer?
Low to Moderate
Moderately High
Very High
Moderately Low
The six riskometer levels are Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High. 'Moderately Low' is not a riskometer level.
The Potential Risk Class (PRC) matrix for debt schemes classifies a scheme on the basis of:
Its maximum interest rate risk and maximum credit risk
Its past three-year returns and expense ratio
The size of its AUM and number of investors
The fund manager's experience and tenure

The PRC matrix shows the maximum interest rate risk (measured by Macaulay duration) and maximum credit risk (measured by a credit risk value) the scheme may take, so investors know its risk limits in advance.
Which change would NOT be treated as a change in a scheme's fundamental attributes?
Change in the type of scheme from open-ended to closed-ended
Change in the scheme's investment objective
Replacement of the scheme's fund manager
Change in the terms of issue, such as fees and loads affecting investors

Fundamental attributes include the type of scheme, investment objective and terms of issue. A change of fund manager is disclosed, but it does not require giving unitholders an exit option without load.
Changes to an SID between its periodic updates are communicated through:
A fresh new fund offer
A Consolidated Account Statement
A letter to SEBI only
An addendum to the document
When information in the SID changes, the AMC issues an addendum that is published and becomes part of the SID until the document is fully updated.
A scheme's annual report (or its abridged version) must be sent or made available to unitholders within:
Four months from the end of the financial year
Two weeks from the end of the financial year
Twelve months from the end of the financial year
One week after the scheme's NFO closes
SEBI requires mutual funds to publish annual reports, and make abridged reports available to unitholders, within four months of the close of the financial year.
Which type of scheme is required to disclose its portfolio every fortnight, in addition to monthly disclosure?
Equity schemes
Index funds tracking Nifty
Debt schemes
ELSS schemes
To improve transparency on credit and liquidity risk, SEBI requires debt schemes to disclose portfolios fortnightly. Other schemes disclose portfolios monthly and half-yearly.
Which SEBI-prescribed document presents key scheme information in a standard, machine-readable format on AMC and AMFI websites?
Statement of Additional Information
Scheme Summary Document
Key Information Memorandum
Consolidated Account Statement
The Scheme Summary Document captures key data points of every scheme, such as fund manager, benchmark, loads and AUM, in a standard machine-readable format, making comparison across schemes easier.

Fund Distribution and Channel Management.overview: This chapter explains how mutual fund schemes reach investors and how distributors are regulated and paid. It covers ARN and EUIN, the NISM certification and continuing education needed to keep an ARN valid, trail commission (upfront commission is not permitted), direct and regular plans, and the difference between a distributor and an investment adviser. Also revise channels such as banks, national distributors, stock exchange platforms, MF Utility and execution-only platforms, plus rules on how distributors may describe themselves.
questions: Under current SEBI norms, mutual fund distributors are paid:
Only upfront commission at the time of purchase
A fixed fee directly by SEBI
Only trail-based commission, with no upfront commission
A share of the scheme's capital gains
SEBI requires that all commissions be paid as trail from the scheme's expenses, without upfront payments. This reduces the incentive for churning investors across schemes.
An investor who invests in a mutual fund through a SEBI-registered investment adviser (who charges a fee) will normally be allotted units of the:
Direct plan
Regular plan
IDCW plan
Institutional plan
RIAs are paid fees by clients and do not earn commissions, so their clients invest in direct plans, which carry lower expenses. Regular plans include distributor commission.
A distributor's NISM certificate is about to expire. To keep the ARN valid, the distributor can:
Simply pay the renewal fee to AMFI and continue, without any further step
Re-take the exam or complete the prescribed CPE
Ask any AMC to extend the certificate
Continue selling for two more years without action
ARN renewal requires a valid NISM certification, which can be renewed by re-taking the exam or attending the prescribed CPE programme before expiry.
An Execution-Only Platform (EOP) in the mutual fund context is a platform that:
Provides personalised investment advice for a fee
Distributes regular plans and earns commission
Manages portfolios on a discretionary basis
Facilitates transactions in direct plans without providing advice

SEBI's EOP framework covers platforms that only execute transactions in direct plans. They neither advise nor earn distribution commission, so they cannot be used as disguised advisory or distribution channels.
MF Utility (MFU) is best described as:
A shared platform to transact across many fund houses
A regulatory body under SEBI that approves new fund offers before they are launched
A credit rating agency for debt schemes
An NBFC that lends against mutual fund units
MFU is an industry-backed shared services platform that lets investors and distributors transact in schemes of many participating AMCs through a single account number and form.
A registered mutual fund distributor who is not an RIA wants to print business cards. Which description is appropriate?
Independent Financial Adviser
Mutual Fund Distributor, with the ARN mentioned
Investment Adviser, SEBI-certified
Wealth Adviser and Portfolio Manager

SEBI and AMFI require distributors to describe themselves as 'Mutual Fund Distributor' and not use terms like 'adviser' that suggest advisory registration. This avoids misleading investors about their role.
Before a distributor can sell a particular AMC's schemes and earn commission, the distributor must:
Obtain a separate licence from RBI
Own a minimum number of the AMC's shares
Invest personally in every scheme sold
Be empanelled with that AMC
Each AMC empanels distributors after checking ARN and other details. Only empanelled distributors receive commission from that AMC for business they bring in.
Stock exchange platforms for mutual fund transactions, such as BSE StAR MF and NSE's NMF platform, allow:
Only institutional investors to buy closed-ended schemes
AMCs to borrow money from each other
Brokers and distributors to process purchases and redemptions for clients
Investors to trade units with each other at negotiated prices
These exchange platforms provide order routing for subscription and redemption of open-ended schemes, in demat or statement-of-account form, through brokers and mutual fund distributors.

NAV, TER and Pricing of Units.overview: This chapter explains how a scheme's Net Asset Value is computed, how expenses are charged through the Total Expense Ratio, and at what price units are bought and redeemed. Revise the NAV formula, daily accrual of expenses, SEBI's slab-based TER limits, exit load and its effect on redemption proceeds, valuation principles for debt securities, NAV publication timelines and how IDCW payouts or reinvestment affect NAV and units. Expect several short calculations.
questions: A scheme has investments and accrued income totalling ₹612 crore, liabilities of ₹12 crore and 40 crore units outstanding. Its NAV is:
NAV = (assets − liabilities) / units = (612 − 12) / 40 = ₹15.00. ₹15.30 ignores the liabilities, and ₹14.70 subtracts them twice.
SEBI's limits on the Total Expense Ratio of open-ended schemes are structured so that:
Every scheme can charge the same flat 2.5% expense ratio
The maximum permitted TER falls as a scheme's AUM grows
TER rises as AUM grows, to reward large schemes
TER can be decided freely by the AMC each month
TER limits are slab-based: higher AUM slabs carry lower maximum percentages, so investors benefit from economies of scale as schemes grow.
A scheme with ₹1,000 crore of assets has a TER of 1.5% a year. Roughly how much expense is accrued each day (365-day year)?
About ₹1.50 crore
About ₹41.1 lakh
About ₹4.11 lakh
About ₹12.50 lakh
Annual expense = 1,000 crore × 1.5% = ₹15 crore. Daily accrual = 15 crore / 365 ≈ ₹4.11 lakh. Expenses are accrued daily, so the NAV is always shown net of them.
An investor redeems 1,000 units at an NAV of ₹50 when a 1% exit load applies. The redemption proceeds (before taxes) are:
Redemption price = NAV × (1 − exit load) = 50 × 0.99 = ₹49.50. For 1,000 units the proceeds are ₹49,500. Exit load reduces, never increases, the amount paid.
How are most debt securities held by mutual fund schemes valued for NAV purposes?
At the price paid by the scheme, until maturity of the bond
Using prices from independent valuation agencies
At face value, irrespective of the market conditions
At a price decided by the fund manager each day
To ensure fair and consistent NAVs, debt securities are valued using prices provided by independent valuation agencies. Holding at cost or face value would hide market movements.
By what time must the NAV of most open-ended schemes be published on AMC and AMFI websites for each business day?
9:00 am on the next business day
The end of the following week
11:00 pm on the same business day
Only at month end
SEBI requires NAVs of open-ended schemes to be uploaded on the AMC and AMFI websites by 11 pm each business day (special timelines apply to some schemes such as fund of funds investing overseas).
An investor holds 2,000 units under the IDCW reinvestment option. The scheme declares IDCW of ₹1.20 per unit and the ex-IDCW NAV is ₹24. Ignoring tax, how many additional units are allotted?
100 units
120 units
96 units
48 units
Amount reinvested = 2,000 × 1.20 = ₹2,400. Units allotted = 2,400 / 24 = 100. Reinvestment uses the ex-IDCW NAV, so total investment value is unchanged.
Which of the following is NOT charged to the scheme within its TER?
Fees paid to the custodian
Trail commission paid to distributors in a regular plan
Fees paid to the registrar and transfer agent
Marketing costs of the AMC beyond permitted limits
Only permitted expenses within SEBI limits may be charged to the scheme; any excess must be borne by the AMC. Custodian fees, RTA fees and distributor trail are standard scheme expenses.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers how mutual fund investments are taxed in India. Revise how equity-oriented schemes are defined, the holding periods for short- and long-term gains, the current rates on equity gains (20% short-term, 12.5% long-term above the annual exemption of ₹1.25 lakh), slab-rate taxation of most debt fund gains on units bought after March 2023, treatment of IDCW, set-off rules for capital losses, grandfathering of pre-2018 equity gains, and why switches are taxable events. Because limits change in Budgets, read the latest rules before the exam.
questions: Short-term capital gains on units of an equity-oriented fund, sold on or after 23 July 2024, are taxed at:
The investor's slab rate
Since 23 July 2024, STCG on equity-oriented fund units (held 12 months or less) on which STT is paid is taxed at 20%, up from the earlier 15%.
Long-term capital gains on equity-oriented fund units are currently taxed at:
10% on gains above ₹1 lakh in a financial year
20% with indexation benefit
12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year
Nil, as long-term equity gains are exempt
From 23 July 2024, LTCG on equity-oriented funds is taxed at 12.5% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh in a year. The earlier rule was 10% on gains above ₹1 lakh.
An investor bought units of a debt fund (investing more than 65% in debt) in 2024 and sells them after four years. The gain is:
Long-term, taxed at 20% with indexation
Long-term, taxed at 12.5% without indexation
Fully exempt after three years
Treated as short-term and taxed at the investor's slab rate
For specified debt-oriented funds bought after 1 April 2023, gains are deemed short-term irrespective of holding period and taxed at slab rates. Indexation benefits do not apply.
An investor switches from the regular plan to the direct plan of the same scheme. For tax purposes, this switch is:
Ignored, as the scheme remains the same
A redemption plus a fresh purchase, so gains may be taxed
Treated as a gift between plans
Tax-exempt only for equity schemes
Regular and direct plans are separate plans with different NAVs, so a switch is a sale of units in one plan and a purchase in another. Any gain is taxable and exit load may apply.
For equity fund units bought before 1 February 2018 and sold later, the cost of acquisition for computing LTCG is:
Always the actual purchase cost paid, without considering any market value adjustment
The NAV on 1 April 2001
Higher of actual cost and 31 Jan 2018 FMV (capped at sale value)
Zero, since gains up to 2018 are taxable
Under grandfathering, gains accrued up to 31 January 2018 are protected. Cost is taken as the higher of actual cost and the lower of FMV on 31 January 2018 and the sale value.
A short-term capital loss on mutual fund units can be set off against:
Only short-term capital gains
Salary income in the same year
Any income, including interest
Both short-term and long-term capital gains
Short-term capital losses can be set off against both STCG and LTCG. Long-term capital losses can be set off only against LTCG. Capital losses cannot be set off against salary.
An investor's LTCG on equity fund units in a financial year is ₹2,00,000 and there are no other equity gains. Ignoring cess and surcharge, the tax payable is:
Taxable gain = 2,00,000 − 1,25,000 exemption = ₹75,000. Tax at 12.5% = ₹9,375. ₹25,000 wrongly applies 12.5% to the whole gain.
For a resident investor, IDCW received from a mutual fund is:
Added to income and taxed at the investor's applicable slab rate
Fully tax-free in the investor's hands
Taxed at a flat 10% irrespective of the investor's total income for the year
Taxed only when units are finally redeemed
Since the abolition of dividend distribution tax in 2020, IDCW is taxable in the hands of the investor at slab rates, with TDS deducted by the fund above the prescribed threshold.

Investor Services.overview: This chapter covers what happens after an investor decides to invest: NFO timelines and allotment, cut-off times and applicable NAV, systematic plans (SIP, STP, SWP), statements, KYC and PAN requirements, nomination and transmission, minors' folios, and NRI investments. Revise the special NAV rule for liquid and overnight funds, the treatment of micro investments, timelines for statements and the steps when a minor turns major. Practise SIP average-cost calculations.
questions: Units of a new fund offer must be allotted to investors within how many business days of the NFO closing?
15 business days
5 business days
30 business days
1 business day
SEBI requires allotment of units and dispatch of statements within five business days of the NFO closure, so investors can begin transacting soon after.
An investor invests in a liquid fund at 1:00 pm on a Friday; funds are credited to the scheme before the cut-off. Monday is a business day. Which NAV applies?
NAV of Friday
NAV of Monday
NAV of Thursday
NAV of Sunday, the day before the next business day

For liquid and overnight funds, an application before 1:30 pm with funds realised gets the NAV of the day immediately preceding the next business day. Here that is Sunday, so the investor earns weekend returns.
The sole holder of a folio has died and a nominee is registered. To get the units, the nominee should normally submit:
A transmission request with the death certificate and the nominee's KYC
A fresh NFO application in the deceased's name
A court succession certificate and indemnity bond in every case, regardless of nominee
A redemption request signed by the deceased

Where a valid nominee exists, transmission is simple: the nominee submits the transmission form, death certificate and own KYC. Succession certificates are needed only when there is no nominee and amounts are large.
When a minor unitholder attains majority, what must happen to the folio?
The units are automatically redeemed and paid to the guardian
The guardian continues to operate it for five more years
It must be changed to major status; until then it is frozen
Nothing changes; the guardian keeps operating the folio
On attaining majority, the investor must submit the change-of-status request with own KYC and bank details. Until then the folio is frozen for transactions, and SIPs registered by the guardian stop.
An investor holds mutual fund units but has made no transaction for several months. How often will a Consolidated Account Statement still be sent?
Only when the investor asks for it in writing
Every week, by email only
Never, until a new transaction is made
Every half-year
Investors who transact receive a CAS for that month. Those without any transaction still receive a CAS every half-year showing holdings and their value, so records stay up to date.
An NRI wants to invest so that both principal and gains can be taken abroad. The investment should be made through:
An NRE account
An NRO account
A resident savings account
A cash payment at the AMC office
Investments routed through the NRE account (or FCNR) are repatriable. Investments from an NRO account are generally non-repatriable, subject to permitted annual remittance limits.
Small SIP investments up to ₹50,000 a year per investor per fund house can be made without PAN through:
A cash deposit with any bank branch
A simple self-declaration of income on the form
PAN-exempt KYC (PEKRN) registration under the micro investment route
The investor's Aadhaar number printed on the cheque
Micro investments up to ₹50,000 a year (including micro SIPs) are exempt from PAN if the investor completes PAN-exempt KYC and obtains a PEKRN. Other KYC norms continue to apply.
An investor puts ₹2,000 a month through a SIP for three months at NAVs of ₹16, ₹20 and ₹25. What is the average cost per unit (to two decimals)?
Units bought = 125 + 100 + 80 = 305. Average cost = 6,000 / 305 = ₹19.67, below the simple average NAV of ₹20.33 because more units are bought when NAV is low.

Risk, Return and Performance of Funds.overview: This chapter explains how mutual fund returns are measured and how risk is assessed. Revise absolute, annualised and compounded returns, and risk measures such as standard deviation, beta, modified duration, credit rating and downside deviation. Learn the risk-adjusted measures: Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino and Jensen's alpha, and which risk each one uses. Understand interest rate, credit, reinvestment and liquidity risk in debt funds, and practise short calculations of risk-adjusted performance.
questions: A fund returned 13% while the risk-free rate was 6%. Its beta is 1.4. What is its Treynor ratio?
Treynor ratio = (fund return − risk-free rate) / beta = (13 − 6) / 1.4 = 5.0. It measures excess return per unit of systematic risk, unlike Sharpe, which uses total risk.
A fund returned 15%, the market returned 12%, the risk-free rate was 6% and the fund's beta is 1.2. What is the fund's Jensen's alpha?
Expected return (CAPM) = 6 + 1.2 × (12 − 6) = 13.2%. Alpha = 15 − 13.2 = 1.8%. Simply comparing with the market (3%) ignores the fund's higher beta.
Which measure best indicates how sensitive a debt fund's NAV is to a change in interest rates?
Standard deviation of equity returns
Modified duration
Credit rating of the portfolio
Expense ratio of the scheme
Modified duration estimates the percentage change in price for a 1% change in yield. A higher modified duration means larger NAV swings when interest rates move.
The Sortino ratio differs from the Sharpe ratio because it uses:
Beta instead of standard deviation
The benchmark return instead of the risk-free rate
Gross return before deducting expenses
Only downside deviation as the measure of risk
Sortino penalises only harmful volatility, using downside deviation below a target return. Sharpe uses total standard deviation, which also counts upside volatility as risk.
Reinvestment risk for a debt investor is highest when:
Rates fall and coupons are reinvested at lower yields
Interest rates are rising steadily and new bonds are being issued at higher coupons
The bond is a zero-coupon bond held to maturity
Inflation is falling with stable interest rates

Reinvestment risk is the risk that cash flows received are reinvested at lower rates. It bites when rates fall. A zero-coupon bond held to maturity has no interim cash flows, so it has no reinvestment risk.
The 'maximum drawdown' of a fund refers to:
The highest NAV the fund has ever reached
The largest fall in value from a peak to a subsequent trough
The largest single-day redemption by investors
The maximum exit load the fund may charge
Maximum drawdown measures the worst peak-to-trough decline over a period. It shows how much an investor could have lost by buying at the top, which standard deviation alone does not reveal.
A fund's NAV rose from ₹10 to ₹13 in six months. What is its simple annualised return?
Absolute return = 3/10 = 30% over six months. Simple annualised return = 30% × (12/6) = 60%. The compounded annualised figure would be 69%, which is a different measure.
Credit risk in a debt fund is best gauged by looking at:
The scheme's modified duration
The number of investors in the scheme
The credit ratings of the securities in the portfolio
The scheme's beta relative to Nifty 50
Credit ratings indicate the likelihood of issuers paying interest and principal on time. Lower-rated holdings mean higher credit risk; duration measures interest rate risk instead.

Mutual Fund Scheme Performance.overview: This chapter explains how to evaluate a scheme's performance fairly. Revise the use of appropriate benchmarks (TRI for equity, relevant debt indices for debt), peer-group comparison within the same category, point-to-point versus rolling returns, CAGR calculation, tracking difference and tracking error for index funds and ETFs, and pitfalls such as survivorship bias. For debt funds, understand how portfolio yield and expenses indicate potential returns. Expect numerical questions on CAGR and tracking difference.
questions: When comparing a scheme's performance with other schemes, the peer group should consist of:
All mutual fund schemes in the industry
Schemes managed by the same fund manager
Schemes launched in the same calendar year
Schemes in the same SEBI category with similar objectives
Peer comparison is meaningful only when schemes share objectives, asset allocation and risk, which is why SEBI categories are used. Comparing across categories mixes very different risks.
Why are rolling returns considered more reliable than a single point-to-point return?
They always show higher returns than point-to-point figures
They reduce the effect of the chosen start and end dates
They are calculated only during bull markets
They exclude the impact of the expense ratio
Point-to-point returns depend heavily on the chosen dates. Rolling returns average performance over many overlapping periods, giving a better picture of consistency.
The most suitable benchmark for a liquid fund is:
The Nifty 50 Total Return Index
A 10-year government bond index
A liquid or money market debt index
The price of gold in rupees
A liquid fund invests in very short-term debt, so its benchmark should be a liquid or money market index with similar maturity and credit profile.
An index fund returned 11.4% in a year while its benchmark TRI returned 12.0%. The tracking difference is:
Tracking difference = fund return − index return = 11.4 − 12.0 = −0.6%. It largely reflects expenses and cash drag. Tracking error is a different measure: the variability of these differences.
When an AMC presents a scheme's past performance in its communications, it must show it:
Only for the period in which returns were highest
Alongside its benchmark's returns for the same periods
Without any comparison, to avoid confusing investors
Along with a promise of similar future returns
SEBI requires performance to be shown against the benchmark (and an additional benchmark where specified) for standard periods, so investors can judge the scheme's value addition.
Category average returns can look better than reality because schemes that were merged or closed due to poor performance are dropped from the data. This is called:
Recency bias
Confirmation bias
Survivorship bias
Home bias
Survivorship bias arises when only surviving funds are counted. Since weak funds tend to be closed or merged, the average of survivors overstates what investors actually earned.
A scheme's NAV grew from ₹10 to ₹20 over exactly 5 years. Its CAGR is closest to:
CAGR = (20/10)^(1/5) − 1 = 14.87%. Dividing the 100% absolute gain by 5 gives 20%, which ignores compounding.
For a debt scheme that holds bonds to maturity, a good indicator of the likely return is:
The scheme's highest one-day return
The past one-month return annualised
The number of bonds in the portfolio
The portfolio yield to maturity minus the expense ratio
If securities are held to maturity, investors broadly earn the portfolio YTM, less expenses. Short-term past returns can be distorted by price changes from rate movements.

Mutual Fund Scheme Selection.overview: This chapter is about matching schemes to investor needs. Revise how goal, time horizon, risk profile and liquidity needs point to suitable categories, how to choose between active and passive funds, direct and regular plans, and growth, IDCW and SWP options. Also consider fund-level factors such as consistency of performance, expense ratio, fund size relative to its category, and portfolio overlap when holding several schemes. Questions are mostly scenario-based, asking for the most suitable recommendation.
questions: An investor wants to build an emergency fund that must be accessible within a day, with very low risk. The most suitable scheme is:
A liquid fund
A small cap fund
A credit risk fund
A sectoral equity fund
Liquid funds invest in instruments maturing within 91 days, have low volatility and process redemptions quickly, which suits emergency money. Equity and credit risk funds are too volatile.
