A cost-conscious investor who believes most active managers will not beat the market over time would prefer:
A thematic fund focused on one theme
A fund with the highest past one-year return
An index fund or ETF tracking a broad index
A focused fund holding 25 stocks
Passive funds track an index at low cost, avoiding the risk of a manager underperforming. Chasing last year's top performer or thematic bets adds manager and concentration risk.
When choosing between two equity funds in the same category, which factor is the most reliable guide?
Which one topped the one-month return chart
Which one has the newest launch date
Which one has the lowest NAV per unit
Consistent performance versus benchmark across cycles
Consistent performance over full cycles reflects process, not luck. A low NAV does not make a fund cheaper, and short-term rankings change frequently.
A moderate-risk investor needs the money in about three years for a home down payment. Which choice is most appropriate?
A small cap fund for higher growth
A short duration debt fund or conservative hybrid fund
A sector fund that has done well recently
A 10-year gilt fund with constant maturity
A three-year goal with moderate risk calls for limited equity and moderate interest rate risk. Small cap and sectoral funds are too volatile, and a 10-year gilt fund carries high duration risk.
An investor who wants guidance on scheme selection and periodic review from a mutual fund distributor will typically invest in:
The direct plan of the scheme
A closed-ended plan only
The regular plan of the scheme
An ETF through the AMC office
Distributors are paid through trail commission included in the regular plan's TER. Investors who want a distributor's service therefore invest in the regular plan; direct plans carry no commission.
Why might an investor prefer the growth option with an SWP over the IDCW option for regular cash flow?
IDCW payouts are guaranteed by the AMC every month, whereas SWP amounts can never be fixed
SWP withdrawals are always fully tax-free for every investor
The IDCW option does not allow redemption at any time
SWP controls amount and timing; only the gain part is taxed
IDCW amounts depend on the AMC's decision and are fully taxable at slab rates. SWP lets the investor fix the amount and date, and tax applies only to the capital gain component.
A very large AUM can be a concern mainly for which type of scheme?
A liquid fund
A small cap fund
A Nifty 50 index fund
An overnight fund

Small cap stocks have limited liquidity. A very large small cap fund may struggle to buy or sell without moving prices, which can hurt returns. Large-cap index funds and liquid funds handle size more easily.
An investor holds three different large cap funds. The main drawback of this choice is:
High portfolio overlap, giving limited extra diversification
A higher tax rate that applies once an investor holds more than one large cap fund
A lock-in on each additional large cap fund
SEBI's ban on holding more than one large cap fund
Large cap funds draw from the same top 100 stocks, so three such funds often hold similar shares. The investor adds complexity and cost without much extra diversification.

Investment Landscape.overview: This chapter introduces basic investing ideas for first-time investors: why saving alone is not enough, how inflation reduces purchasing power, and the difference between saving and investing. It covers common asset classes (equity, debt, gold, real estate, cash), their typical risk and return, and core concepts such as liquidity, compounding, diversification and matching investments to goals and time horizons. Questions are simple and practical; practise compound interest and inflation calculations with small numbers.
questions: Money kept idle in a locker for 10 years while prices rise by about 6% a year will:
Keep exactly the same purchasing power
Lose purchasing power over time
Grow in value at the rate of inflation
Earn interest from the Reserve Bank
Cash earns nothing, so rising prices reduce what the same amount can buy. This is why savings need to be invested in assets that aim to beat inflation.
Which asset class gives a part-owner's share in a company's profits and growth?
Fixed deposits
Government bonds
Savings bank accounts
Equity
Equity shares represent ownership, so shareholders share in profits and growth (and losses). Deposits and bonds are loans to the issuer that pay interest instead.
If ₹50,000 is invested at 8% a year compounded annually, what is it worth after 2 years?
Value = 50,000 × 1.08 × 1.08 = ₹58,320. ₹58,000 is simple interest of ₹4,000 a year, which ignores interest earned on interest.
Which of these generally offers the highest long-term return potential along with the highest short-term volatility?
Bank fixed deposits of five years
Treasury bills
Equity shares
Savings bank deposits
Equity has historically offered the highest long-term growth but its prices swing sharply in the short run. Deposits and T-bills are more stable but offer lower returns.
An investor needs money for a child's school fees in six months. Which feature matters most when choosing where to keep this money?
Highest possible long-term growth
Tax benefit under a long lock-in
Exposure to small companies
Safety and liquidity
Short-term goals need money that will be available and not fall in value. Seeking high growth with volatile assets could leave a shortfall exactly when the fees are due.
Gold is often added to a portfolio mainly because it:
Tends to behave differently from equities and can hedge against uncertainty
Pays a fixed rate of interest every year, like a government savings bond held to maturity
Has no price risk at all
Is fully guaranteed by the government
Gold often holds value during market stress or currency weakness, so it can diversify a portfolio. It pays no interest and its price can be volatile.
'Do not put all your eggs in one basket' describes the principle of:
Leverage
Speculation
Diversification
Market timing
Diversification means spreading money across many investments so that a problem in one does not hurt the whole portfolio badly. It reduces risk specific to any single investment.
The main difference between saving and investing is that investing:
Keeps all the money only as cash at home or in a locker, so that it is always within reach
Puts money into assets aiming for growth, accepting some risk
Never involves any risk to capital
Is meant only for very wealthy people
Saving sets aside money from income; investing deploys it into assets such as equity, debt or gold to earn returns, usually with some risk. Anyone can invest small amounts through SIPs.

Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund.overview: This chapter explains what a mutual fund is in simple terms: a pool of money from many investors, managed professionally, with each investor owning units in proportion to the amount invested. Revise the main benefits (diversification, professional management, liquidity, transparency, small ticket sizes), key terms such as NAV, unit, AUM and folio, and the difference between open-ended, closed-ended, active and passive schemes. Also understand basic categories such as equity, debt, hybrid and index funds.
questions: A 'unit' of a mutual fund scheme represents:
A fixed deposit placed with the AMC that earns a stated rate of interest
A loan given by the investor to SEBI
A proportionate share in the scheme's assets
A share in the AMC company's profits
Each unit is a proportional claim on the scheme's net assets. Unitholders do not own shares of the AMC and do not lend money to the fund.
Assets Under Management (AUM) of a scheme refers to:
The total market value of investments managed in the scheme
The minimum investment amount that a new investor must put into the scheme
The AMC's own share capital
The profit earned by the fund manager
AUM is the total value of money the scheme manages on behalf of investors. It changes daily with market movements, purchases and redemptions.
Which of these is an example of a passive fund?
A flexi cap fund selecting stocks freely
An index fund tracking the Nifty 50
A value fund picking cheap stocks
A focused fund holding 25 stocks
A passive fund simply replicates an index without stock selection by the manager. Flexi cap, value and focused funds are actively managed.
How can a small investor with ₹500 a month gain exposure to many companies at once?
By buying one share of every Nifty company
By opening multiple savings accounts
By buying a single small cap share
By investing through a mutual fund SIP
Mutual funds pool money from many investors, so even ₹500 buys a slice of a diversified portfolio. Buying one share of every index company would cost far more.
A debt fund primarily invests in:
Bonds, government securities and money market instruments
Shares of listed companies across large, mid and small caps
Real estate properties
Physical gold and silver
Debt funds lend money by buying fixed income securities and earn interest and price gains. Equity funds buy shares, and gold ETFs hold gold.
Which of the following is TRUE about returns from a mutual fund?
They are guaranteed by the AMC, subject to the scheme completing three years
They depend on the performance of the underlying investments
They are fixed by SEBI every year
They are insured by DICGC
Mutual fund returns are market-linked and are not guaranteed by anyone. DICGC insurance applies to bank deposits, not mutual fund units.
A hybrid fund is one that invests in:
Only overnight money market instruments with a maturity of one business day
Only shares of one sector
Only units of foreign mutual funds
A combination of asset classes such as equity and debt
Hybrid funds mix asset classes, usually equity and debt (sometimes gold), in proportions defined by their SEBI category, aiming to balance growth and stability.
The 'folio' in a mutual fund helps an investor to:
Get a guaranteed return from the AMC on all the schemes held together in that account
Avoid paying any tax on gains
Hold all investments in schemes of one fund house under one account number
Trade units on the stock exchange
A folio number is like an account number with a fund house. All investments in its schemes can be grouped in one folio, which simplifies statements and servicing.

Legal Structure of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter explains who is who in a mutual fund. A mutual fund is set up as a trust by a sponsor; trustees protect unitholders' interests; the AMC manages the money; and service providers such as the custodian, RTA, auditor and collecting banks support operations. Revise the role of each constituent and of AMFI, the industry body that registers distributors and promotes investor awareness. Questions test simple role-matching, so learn one clear line about each entity.
questions: The mutual fund trust is registered with which regulator before it can launch schemes?
RBI
IRDAI
PFRDA
SEBI
Every mutual fund in India must be registered with SEBI under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996. RBI regulates banks, IRDAI insurance and PFRDA pensions.
Which constituent of a mutual fund makes buy and sell decisions for the scheme's portfolio?
The custodian of the fund
The AMC, through its fund managers
The registrar and transfer agent
The investors, by voting each week
The AMC employs fund managers and research analysts who decide which securities to buy and sell in line with the scheme's objective. Investors do not vote on daily decisions.
The statutory auditor of a mutual fund scheme is responsible for:
Selecting the stocks that the scheme buys and deciding when to sell them
Processing investor KYC applications
Auditing the scheme's accounts and reporting on them
Holding the scheme's securities
The auditor examines and reports on the scheme's accounts independently. Stock selection belongs to the AMC, KYC to KRAs and intermediaries, and custody to the custodian.
Which entity is responsible for keeping a check on the AMC to protect unitholders?
The trustees
The distributors
The stock exchanges
The rating agencies
Trustees supervise the AMC and ensure it acts in unitholders' interests and complies with regulations. Distributors sell schemes; exchanges and rating agencies have different roles.
AMFI is best described as:
A government department that regulates AMCs and issues their licences
The industry association of SEBI-registered AMCs
A bank that holds mutual fund money
A company that manages mutual fund schemes
AMFI is an industry body formed by AMCs. It is not a statutory regulator; it registers distributors (ARN), frames codes of conduct and works on investor education.
Banks that receive investors' application money on behalf of a scheme are called:
Custodian banks of the scheme
Sponsor banks
Collecting bankers
Trustee banks
Collecting bankers accept investment money for the scheme at their branches or through electronic channels. A custodian holds the securities, a different role.
The custodian of a mutual fund does NOT do which of the following?
Decide which stocks the scheme should buy
Hold the scheme's securities safely
Settle securities bought and sold
Keep track of corporate actions on holdings
The custodian keeps securities in safe custody, settles trades and tracks corporate actions like dividends and bonuses. Investment decisions are made by the AMC.
In the mutual fund structure, the sponsor is comparable to:
A customer of a bank
An independent auditor
A stock exchange
The promoter of a company
Just as a promoter sets up a company, the sponsor establishes the mutual fund, sets up the trust and the AMC, and must meet SEBI eligibility conditions.

Mutual Fund Products for New Cadre Distr.overview: This chapter covers the simple mutual fund products that new cadre distributors mainly deal with: index funds and ETFs, diversified equity schemes, ELSS, and simple debt and hybrid options. Revise how each product works, its risk level, its suitability, and features such as ELSS lock-in, ETF trading on exchanges and passive tracking of an index. Understand concepts such as tracking error, market capitalisation categories and why diversified funds are less risky than sector funds. Questions often ask which product suits a described investor.
questions: An ETF's price on the stock exchange during the day is determined by:
Buying and selling by investors on the exchange, close to its intraday value
Only the NAV declared by the AMC at the end of the previous business day
A fixed price set by SEBI for each year
The AMC's decision each morning
ETF units trade on exchanges like shares, so their market price moves through the day with demand and supply. Market makers help keep it close to the indicative NAV.
To buy units of an ETF on the exchange, an investor generally needs:
Only a bank fixed deposit account
A loan from the AMC
A demat and trading account
A Public Provident Fund account
ETFs are listed securities, so buying them requires a trading account with a broker and a demat account to hold the units, just like shares.
Which product would suit an investor who wants both a tax deduction under the old regime and long-term equity growth?
An overnight fund
A liquid fund
A gold ETF
An ELSS scheme
ELSS is an equity scheme with a three-year lock-in that qualifies for a tax deduction under the old tax regime. Overnight, liquid and gold ETFs do not offer this deduction.
An index fund's NAV moves slightly differently from its index mainly because of:
The fund manager's stock-picking bets
Expenses and cash holdings of the fund
A guaranteed bonus paid by the AMC
SEBI's daily adjustments to NAV
Index funds copy the index, but expenses, cash for redemptions and timing of trades cause small gaps known as tracking error. They do not involve active stock picking.
A sectoral fund investing only in banking shares is riskier than a diversified equity fund because:
It is not regulated by SEBI
It cannot be redeemed for five years
Its performance depends heavily on one sector
It invests only in government bonds
Concentration in one sector means a downturn in that sector hits the whole portfolio. A diversified fund spreads investments across many sectors.
Which of these is TRUE of a large cap fund?
It invests only in companies ranked 251st and below by full market capitalisation
It must hold at least 50% in bonds
It guarantees returns higher than bank deposits
It invests mainly in the 100 largest companies by market capitalisation
Large cap funds invest at least 80% in the top 100 companies by full market capitalisation, which are generally more established and less volatile than mid or small caps.
An investor starts an ELSS SIP of ₹2,000 a month. When can the instalment invested in March 2026 be redeemed at the earliest?
March 2027
March 2029
March 2031
Any time after March 2026
Each ELSS instalment has its own three-year lock-in from the date of investment. The March 2026 instalment can therefore be redeemed only from March 2029.
A Gold ETF is suitable for an investor who wants:
Exposure to gold prices without holding physical gold
A fixed interest income credited to the bank account on the same date every month
Ownership of gold mining company shares only
A guaranteed return linked to the repo rate
A Gold ETF holds physical gold of defined purity and tracks domestic gold prices. It avoids storage and purity worries but pays no interest.

Scheme Related Information.overview: This chapter explains the documents investors should read before investing: the Scheme Information Document (scheme-specific details), the Statement of Additional Information (fund-house-level details), and the Key Information Memorandum (summary that comes with the application form). It also covers the riskometer, factsheets and periodic portfolio disclosures. Revise which document contains what, what the riskometer conveys, and how investors can use factsheets to track holdings, expenses and performance.
questions: Where would an investor find the exit load applicable to a particular scheme?
In the AMC's annual report only
In the Scheme Information Document and KIM
In the investor's PAN card details
In the stock exchange's daily bulletin
Loads are terms of the offer, so they are disclosed in the SID and summarised in the KIM. Factsheets also usually show the current exit load.
The riskometer of a scheme is meant to help investors:
Find out the exact return that the scheme will deliver over the next one year
Compare tax rates on different schemes
See the distributor's commission
Understand the level of risk in the scheme at a glance
The riskometer shows risk on a six-level scale from Low to Very High. It does not predict returns or show costs.
A monthly factsheet issued by an AMC typically shows:
Holdings, AUM, TER and performance
The personal details of each investor
The names of investors who redeemed
Guaranteed returns for the next year
Factsheets summarise key scheme data such as top holdings, sector mix, AUM, TER, fund manager and performance versus benchmark, helping investors monitor their schemes.
Which document must be given along with every mutual fund application form?
Statement of Additional Information
Annual report of the AMC
Key Information Memorandum
Trust deed of the mutual fund
The KIM, a short summary of the SID, must accompany every application form so that investors see the key features before investing.
An investor wants information about the mutual fund's sponsor, trustees and AMC directors. The most relevant document is the:
Key Information Memorandum
Account statement
Riskometer
Statement of Additional Information
The SAI contains statutory information common to all schemes of the fund house, such as details of the sponsor, AMC, trustees and their directors.
If a scheme's riskometer moves from 'High' to 'Very High', this means:
The assessed risk level of the scheme's portfolio has increased
The scheme's returns are now guaranteed to rise in proportion to the higher level of risk
The scheme will now be closed for redemptions
The scheme's exit load has been removed
Riskometers are reviewed monthly based on the portfolio. A move to Very High shows the portfolio has become riskier, which investors should note.
The investment objective stated in an SID tells the investor:
The exact return the scheme will earn
The tax rate on redemption proceeds
What the scheme aims to achieve and broadly how
The NAV on the date of allotment
The objective describes the scheme's goal, such as long-term capital growth by investing in large cap equity. It does not promise any return.
Periodic disclosure of the scheme's portfolio is useful because it lets investors:
Avoid paying any expense ratio
Check whether the fund follows its stated mandate
Trade the underlying shares directly
Change the scheme's investment objective
By seeing actual holdings, investors can confirm that the scheme invests as promised and judge concentration and credit quality.

Fund Distribution and Channel Management.overview: This chapter covers how mutual funds reach investors and what a new cadre distributor must do. Revise registration requirements (NISM certification and ARN from AMFI), EUIN, the difference between direct and regular plans, how distributors earn trail commission, KYC duties, and ethical selling practices including suitability and avoiding mis-selling. Also know the main channels such as individual distributors, banks, online platforms and stock exchange platforms, and the basics of the AMFI code of conduct.
questions: A distributor's EUIN is unique to:
The scheme in which the investor invests
The investor's bank account
The individual employee who serves the investor
The stock exchange used for transactions
EUIN identifies the specific employee or relationship manager of a distributor who served the investor. It helps track advice quality and prevent mis-selling.
A new cadre distributor's main source of income from AMCs is:
Trail commission based on the investor's assets
A fixed salary paid by AMFI
A share of the investor's capital gains
A fee collected from SEBI
Distributors earn trail commission, a percentage of the assets their clients hold in regular plans, paid periodically while the investment remains.
An investor in the regular plan pays a slightly higher expense ratio than in the direct plan because:
The regular plan holds riskier securities
The regular plan includes distribution commission
The direct plan is subsidised by SEBI
The direct plan does not pay any custodian fees
Both plans hold the same portfolio. The regular plan's TER includes trail commission to the distributor, so its NAV grows slightly slower.
Before recommending a scheme, a distributor should first:
Recommend the scheme that paid the highest return last month
Recommend whatever the AMC is promoting this quarter
Ask the investor to sign a blank form
Understand the investor's goals, horizon and risk appetite
Suitable advice starts with knowing the investor. Recommending based on recent returns or AMC campaigns, or taking blank signed forms, can lead to mis-selling.
Which of these is an unethical practice for a distributor?
Encouraging frequent switching to earn more commission
Explaining the risks of the scheme clearly
Giving the investor the KIM with the form
Keeping records of the investor's risk profile
Churning investors between schemes for higher commission harms investors and violates the AMFI code of conduct. The other practices are good conduct.
An investor can transact in mutual funds without any distributor by:
Calling SEBI's helpline
Buying the direct plan from the AMC
Writing to the stock exchange
Asking the custodian bank
Direct plans can be bought from the AMC's own website, office or app, or through RTA and other direct channels, without a distributor and without commission.
When a bank sells mutual fund schemes to its customers, it acts as a:
Trustee of the mutual fund
Custodian of the investor's units
Regulator of the AMC
Mutual fund distributor holding an ARN
Banks distribute mutual funds as corporate distributors with an ARN, and their staff who sell must be NISM-certified with an EUIN.
Which detail must a distributor's application form submission carry so that commission is paid correctly?
The investor's mobile network provider
The fund manager's name
The distributor's ARN code
The investor's employer's PAN
The ARN code on the form links the transaction to the distributor, so the AMC knows whom to pay trail commission. Without it the investment goes into the direct plan.

Performance of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter explains simple ways to judge how a mutual fund has performed. Revise how NAV changes and IDCW payouts make up total return, absolute versus annualised return, the role of benchmarks, comparing schemes only within the same category, and why expenses matter over long periods. Understand that past performance does not guarantee future results and that consistency over time is more meaningful than a single good year. Practise basic return calculations with whole numbers.
questions: A scheme's NAV rose from ₹40 to ₹46 in one year with no IDCW. What is the return?
Return = (46 − 40) / 40 × 100 = 15%. ₹6 is the gain in rupees, not the percentage, and 13% wrongly divides by the ending NAV.
An investor bought a unit at ₹20, received an IDCW of ₹1, and the unit is now worth ₹21. What is the total return for the year?
Total return = (21 − 20 + 1) / 20 × 100 = 10%. Ignoring the IDCW would give only 5%, which understates what the investor earned.
Which statement about past performance is correct?
It guarantees at least the same return next year
It is the only factor needed to choose a fund
It does not guarantee future returns
It is fixed by SEBI for every category
Markets change and so do fund returns. Past performance is useful for judging consistency, but it is not a promise of future results, as every scheme document states.
Two equity funds hold the same portfolio. Fund A has a TER of 0.5% and Fund B 1.5%. Over 20 years, Fund A will most likely:
Deliver higher returns because of lower costs
Deliver lower returns because cheap funds perform worse
Deliver exactly the same returns as Fund B
Be closed by SEBI for charging too little
With identical portfolios, the only difference is cost. A 1% lower expense each year compounds into a meaningful difference over 20 years.
A scheme's benchmark is used to:
Decide the investor's tax rate
Judge if the manager added value
Fix the exit load of the scheme
Calculate the distributor's commission
A benchmark represents the market the scheme invests in. Beating it after costs shows the manager added value; lagging it shows the opposite.
Investment of ₹1,00,000 grew to ₹1,50,000 in 3 years. The absolute return is:
Absolute return = (1,50,000 − 1,00,000) / 1,00,000 = 50%. 16.7% is a simple yearly average, and 14.5% is the compounded annual rate, both different measures.
Which comparison is appropriate when evaluating a large cap fund?
Comparing it with large cap peers and index
Comparing it with a liquid fund's return
Comparing it with a bank savings rate only
Comparing it with a gold ETF's return
Fair comparison needs similar risk and objectives. A large cap fund should be compared with its category peers and a large cap benchmark.
A fund that returned 40% last year but lost heavily in other years may be less attractive than one with steady returns because:
High returns are not allowed under SEBI rules
Steady funds are guaranteed by the AMC
A 40% return is always taxed at a higher rate
Consistency is a better guide than one year
One outstanding year can be luck or due to a short-lived theme. Consistent performance across years and market conditions is a more reliable signal of quality.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers the basic tax rules that new investors and distributors should know. Revise how equity-oriented schemes are defined (at least 65% in domestic equity), the 12-month holding period for long-term equity gains, current tax rates on equity gains, taxation of IDCW at slab rates, the ELSS deduction under the old regime, and that switches between schemes are treated as redemptions. Also know that STT applies on redemption of equity-oriented units. Because rates change in Budgets, check the latest figures before the exam.
questions: A scheme qualifies as 'equity-oriented' for tax purposes if it invests at least what share of its assets in domestic equity shares?
An equity-oriented fund must invest at least 65% in equity shares of domestic listed companies. Such schemes get the concessional tax treatment applicable to equity.
An investor sells equity fund units after 18 months at a gain. The gain is treated as:
Short-term capital gain
Income from salary
Long-term capital gain
Business income
For equity-oriented funds, units held for more than 12 months are long-term capital assets. Eighteen months exceeds this, so the gain is long-term.
IDCW received by a resident investor from a mutual fund is taxed:
At a flat 5% for all investors
Only if it exceeds ₹10 lakh a year
Never, as it is exempt income
At the investor's income tax slab rate
IDCW is added to the investor's income and taxed at the applicable slab rate. The fund may also deduct TDS above a threshold.
An investor switches from an equity fund to a debt fund of the same AMC. For tax purposes, the switch is:
A tax-free transfer within the same AMC
Treated as a redemption, so capital gains tax may apply
Taxed only when the debt fund is sold
Treated as a fresh gift to the AMC
A switch is a sale of units in one scheme and a purchase in another. Any gain on the units switched out is taxable, and exit load may also apply.
Securities Transaction Tax on mutual funds is charged on:
Purchase of units of debt schemes
Redemption of units of liquid funds
Redemption of units of equity-oriented schemes
IDCW paid by all schemes
STT applies to the sale (redemption) of units of equity-oriented funds, at a very small rate collected by the fund. Debt fund transactions do not attract STT.
Investment in ELSS is eligible for a tax deduction only for taxpayers who:
Opt for the new tax regime
Are non-residents
Earn only capital gains
Opt for the old tax regime
The new tax regime does not allow most deductions, including the ELSS deduction. Taxpayers must choose the old regime to claim this benefit.
A long-term capital loss on mutual fund units can be set off against:
Any salary income
Only long-term capital gains
Interest from fixed deposits
Short-term gains and salary
Long-term capital losses can only be set off against long-term capital gains, in the same year or the next eight years. They cannot reduce salary or interest income.
Who deducts TDS on IDCW paid to a resident investor, where applicable?
The mutual fund, before paying the IDCW
The investor's employer
The investor's bank, at the time of credit
The distributor, from its commission
The mutual fund deducts TDS on IDCW above the prescribed threshold before paying it out, and the investor can claim credit for it while filing the return.

Investor Services.overview: This chapter covers how investors open accounts and transact with mutual funds. Revise KYC requirements (PAN, address proof, KYC through a KRA), cut-off times and applicable NAV, systematic plans (SIP, STP, SWP), switches, redemptions and their timelines, account statements, nomination, and how to update details such as bank account or address. Know the purpose of each systematic plan and the basic steps when an investor dies or when details change.
questions: A KYC done through a KYC Registration Agency (KRA) allows an investor to:
Skip PAN for all future investments
Invest across intermediaries without repeating KYC
Avoid paying any tax on mutual fund gains
Invest only in the schemes of one AMC
KYC recorded with a KRA is shared across SEBI-registered intermediaries, so investors do not have to repeat the full process for each AMC or broker.
An investor wants to invest ₹5,000 every month automatically into an equity scheme. The suitable facility is a:
Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP)
One-time lumpsum purchase
Switch from another scheme
Systematic Investment Plan (SIP)
A SIP debits a fixed amount from the bank account at regular intervals and buys units, building discipline and averaging purchase cost over time.
An investor with a lump sum in a liquid fund wants to move ₹10,000 every month into an equity fund. The suitable facility is a:
Systematic Transfer Plan (STP)
Systematic Investment Plan from the bank
Systematic Withdrawal Plan to the bank
Fresh NFO application each month
An STP transfers a fixed amount periodically from one scheme to another of the same fund house, letting the lump sum enter equity gradually.
Redemption proceeds of most equity schemes are normally paid to the investor within:
15 working days
30 days
3 working days
6 months
SEBI requires most schemes to pay redemption proceeds within three working days of the request (with some exceptions for schemes investing overseas or in special situations).
Why should an investor register a nominee in a mutual fund folio?
To get a higher NAV on redemption
To avoid paying exit load
To allow the nominee to trade on the investor's behalf now
To simplify transmission after the investor's death
A nominee can claim the units easily after the holder's death, avoiding lengthy legal processes. A nominee has no rights while the investor is alive.
An investor wants to change the bank account registered in a folio. The request should be made:
With a written request and proof of the new bank account
By telling the distributor on a phone call only
By writing a new bank number on a redemption form
By sending an SMS to SEBI
Change of bank mandate requires a signed request with proof such as a cancelled cheque or bank statement. This protects investors from fraud.
Under the growth option of a scheme, the investor's gains are:
Paid out as cash every month
Converted to fixed deposits
Retained in the scheme and reflected in a rising NAV
Distributed among other unitholders
In the growth option, income and gains stay invested, so the NAV increases. Gains are realised only when units are redeemed.
For an equity scheme, a purchase of ₹50,000 received by 3 pm on a business day, with funds credited before the cut-off, gets:
The NAV of the previous day
The NAV of the same day
The NAV fixed at the NFO
The NAV of the next month
For equity schemes, the applicable NAV depends on when funds are realised in the scheme's account. If the money is available before the 3 pm cut-off, the same day's NAV applies.

Legal and Regulatory Environment.overview: This chapter explains how mutual funds are regulated in India and how investors are protected. SEBI is the regulator under the SEBI Act, 1992 and the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996; AMFI sets industry codes of conduct for AMCs and distributors. Revise investor rights (information, timely payment, exit option on fundamental changes), the grievance route from AMC to SCORES to online dispute resolution, and what distributors must and must not do under the code of conduct.
questions: If an AMC does not resolve an investor's complaint satisfactorily, the investor can escalate it online through:
The RBI Integrated Ombudsman
The Insurance Ombudsman
SEBI's SCORES platform
The local police station
SCORES is SEBI's online grievance system for complaints against listed companies and intermediaries, including mutual funds. Unresolved disputes can then go to online dispute resolution.
Which of these is an investor's right in a mutual fund scheme?
Timely payment of redemption proceeds
Receiving a guaranteed minimum return
Choosing the stocks the fund buys
Getting back losses from the AMC
Investors have rights to information, timely payment and fair treatment. Returns are not guaranteed and investment decisions remain with the AMC.
AMFI's code of conduct for distributors requires them to:
Guarantee returns on equity schemes
Recommend suitable schemes and disclose key facts
Promise to buy back units at a higher price
Share the investor's details with other agents
The code requires distributors to act in investors' interest, give suitable advice, provide scheme documents and keep information confidential.
Which regulator's rules govern how mutual funds may advertise their schemes?
AMFI alone, with no SEBI role
RBI
Ministry of Finance only
SEBI
SEBI's mutual fund regulations include an advertisement code that sets rules on disclosures, standard warnings and performance presentation. AMFI issues supporting industry guidelines.
Mutual funds in India are mainly regulated under:
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Insurance Act, 1938
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 set rules for sponsors, trustees, AMCs, schemes, investments and disclosures. Banking and insurance laws apply to other sectors.
A distributor collects cash of ₹1 lakh from a client and promises to deposit it into a scheme later. This practice is:
Acceptable if the distributor gives a handwritten receipt
Not appropriate; money must go directly to the scheme
Encouraged to save the investor's time
Mandatory for investors without bank accounts
Investor money must go directly to the scheme through permitted payment modes, not through the distributor. Collecting money personally is risky and against the code of conduct.
If an AMC proposes to merge a scheme with another scheme, changing its fundamental attributes, existing investors must be:
Forced to remain invested in the merged scheme
Charged a higher exit load to discourage exit
Paid a guaranteed bonus by the AMC
Given an option to exit without exit load
A merger that changes fundamental attributes requires informing unitholders and offering them an exit at NAV without load during the specified period.
A dispute with a mutual fund remains unresolved even after SCORES. The investor can next use:
The Consumer Court only, with no other route
A complaint to AMFI's distributor desk
The securities market Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) platform
A complaint to the stock exchange where units are not listed
SEBI's ODR mechanism allows investors to resolve disputes with market intermediaries, including mutual funds, through online conciliation and arbitration.

Investment Landscape.overview: This chapter sets the context for advising investors on sophisticated products. It covers financial goals, risk capacity versus risk appetite, asset classes and their behaviour, asset allocation and rebalancing, and behavioural biases. For SIF distribution, focus on judging whether an investor has the wealth, horizon and understanding to handle long-short strategies. Practise calculations on rebalancing, real returns and compounding, and know how correlation between assets affects portfolio risk.
questions: Two assets have a correlation of −0.3. Combining them in a portfolio will most likely:
Double the portfolio's expected return
Reduce overall portfolio volatility
Remove all market risk from the portfolio, whatever the weights chosen
Increase volatility compared with each asset alone
Assets that do not move together offset part of each other's fluctuations, so portfolio volatility falls below the weighted average. Negative correlation does not remove all risk or double returns.
An investor's risk profile questionnaire shows high willingness to take risk, but she has little savings and needs the money in a year. A distributor should give more weight to her:
High stated risk appetite and her strong wish to earn equity-like returns
Preference for recent top performers
Interest in new fund offers
Limited risk capacity
Risk capacity, the ability to absorb losses, limits what is suitable regardless of willingness. A short horizon and small savings mean she cannot afford large losses.
A portfolio drifts from its target 50:50 equity–debt mix to 65:35 after a rally. Restoring the 50:50 mix by selling equity is called:
Rebalancing
Market timing based on a forecast of the next rally
Averaging down
Tactical overweighting
Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to its strategic mix, which controls risk and enforces 'sell high, buy low' discipline. It is rule-based rather than forecast-based.
An investor feels the pain of a ₹1 lakh loss far more than the pleasure of a ₹1 lakh gain and therefore refuses to sell losing positions. This reflects:
Overconfidence in one's own stock-picking ability and research
Anchoring
Loss aversion
Home bias
Loss aversion means losses hurt more than equal gains please. It often leads investors to hold losers too long in the hope of breaking even.
Which investor is most likely to need a high allocation to liquid, low-risk assets?
A 30-year-old saving for retirement through a monthly SIP over thirty years
One with a 15-year goal and stable income
One with surplus wealth and no near-term needs
One with a large expense due in three months
Money needed soon should not be exposed to market swings. Long horizons and stable incomes allow more equity; near-term needs call for liquidity and safety.
₹10,00,000 grows at 12% a year for 3 years, compounded annually. The ending value is closest to:
Value = 10,00,000 × 1.12³ = ₹14,04,928. ₹13,60,000 is simple interest for three years, which ignores compounding.
Inflation is 6% and a debt investment yields 7% before tax. For an investor in the 30% tax slab, the approximate real post-tax return is:
+4.9%, since tax applies only to the real part of the return
Post-tax yield = 7% × (1 − 0.30) = 4.9%. Subtracting 6% inflation gives about −1.1%. Taxes apply to the full nominal return, which is why high-slab investors can lose purchasing power.
Which asset class typically provides regular income with lower volatility than equity?
Small cap equity
High-quality debt
Sectoral equity funds investing in a single cyclical sector such as metals
Equity derivatives
High-quality bonds pay regular interest and their prices move far less than equities. Small caps, sector funds and derivatives carry much higher volatility.

Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund.overview: This chapter covers the mutual fund concept and SEBI's scheme categories, and introduces the Specialized Investment Fund (SIF) as a separate product within the mutual fund framework. Revise the SIF investment strategies (equity long-short, equity ex-top 100 long-short, sector rotation long-short, debt long-short, sectoral debt long-short, active asset allocator long-short and hybrid long-short) with their key allocation rules, the minimum investment threshold, short exposure limits and the five-level risk band. Also revise regular mutual fund categories that SIFs are compared with.
questions: An SIF's Equity Ex-Top 100 Long-Short strategy must invest at least 65% of its assets in:
Large cap stocks ranked 1 to 100 by full market capitalisation
Government securities
Equity outside the top 100 stocks
Units of other SIFs
As its name suggests, this strategy focuses on companies outside the top 100 by market capitalisation, with at least 65% in such equities, while using limited short positions through derivatives.
Under the SIF framework, a Sector Rotation Long-Short strategy invests at least 80% of its assets in:
Equity of at most four sectors
Equity spread across at least ten sectors in equal weights
Debt of a single sector
Any asset class freely
Sector rotation SIFs concentrate at least 80% in equity and equity-related instruments of a maximum of four sectors, rotating among them, with limited short exposure.
A Hybrid Long-Short SIF must hold at least:
65% in equity and the rest in gold
25% each in equity and in debt
80% in debt and money market instruments, with no equity at all
50% in REITs and InvITs
The hybrid long-short strategy invests at least 25% in equity and at least 25% in debt, with flexibility for the rest and limited unhedged shorts.
How many risk levels does the SIF risk-band use?
Six, the same as the mutual fund riskometer used for regular schemes
Three
Ten
Five
SIF strategies carry a risk-band with five levels (Level 1 lowest to Level 5 highest), distinct from the six-level riskometer used for regular mutual fund schemes.
Which statement about short positions in an SIF is correct?
Unhedged shorts via derivatives are capped
SIFs may short-sell any amount of stock without limits through the cash market
SIFs cannot use derivatives at all
Short positions are allowed only in debt SIFs
SIFs may take unhedged short exposure through derivatives within a set cap (25% of net assets). Derivatives for hedging and rebalancing are permitted in addition.
An AMC already offers one Equity Long-Short SIF strategy. It wants to launch a second Equity Long-Short strategy. Under SEBI norms, this is:
Permitted, provided both strategies have a different fund manager and benchmark
Not permitted
Permitted only for accredited investors
Mandatory once AUM crosses ₹1,000 crore
As with mutual fund categories, an AMC may offer only one strategy in each SIF strategy type, so investors are not confused by near-identical offerings.
The key feature that distinguishes an SIF from a regular equity mutual fund is that an SIF:
Guarantees a minimum return to investors who stay invested for three years or more
Has no minimum investment
Is not regulated by SEBI
Can take limited short positions
SIFs bridge mutual funds and PMS/AIFs by allowing long-short strategies with a higher minimum ticket. Regular mutual funds cannot take unhedged short positions.
A Debt Long-Short SIF is most likely to use which instruments for its short exposure?
Short sale of equity shares in the cash market
Gold futures only
Exchange-traded interest rate derivatives
Bank fixed deposits placed with the AMC's sponsor
Debt long-short strategies take long positions in debt instruments and short exposure through interest rate derivatives, aiming to benefit from views on rates and spreads.

Legal Structure of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter explains the structure that also governs SIFs: the sponsor, the mutual fund trust and trustees, the AMC and service providers such as custodians, RTAs and auditors. SIFs are offered by eligible AMCs of SEBI-registered mutual funds, under the oversight of the same trustees. Revise the duties of trustees and the AMC, independence requirements for boards, AMC eligibility routes for launching SIFs, and the role of the custodian, RTA and fund accountant.
questions: A Specialized Investment Fund is launched and managed by:
A portfolio manager registered under the SEBI PMS Regulations, separately from any mutual fund
A bank's treasury department
An insurance company
An eligible mutual fund AMC
SIFs are set up under the SEBI mutual fund framework by AMCs that meet the eligibility conditions, and are overseen by the mutual fund's trustees.
Under one eligibility route, an AMC may launch SIFs if it has been operating for at least three years with average AUM over the preceding three years of at least:
₹500 crore across all its schemes taken together
₹10,000 crore
₹50 crore
SEBI's first eligibility route requires a track record of at least three years and average AUM of at least ₹10,000 crore in the preceding three years, with no regulatory action in that period.
Who is responsible for ensuring that an AMC launching SIF strategies complies with SEBI regulations and protects investors' interests?
The distributors who sell the strategy and collect application forms from investors
The stock exchange
The trustees
The investors' bankers
Trustees oversee the AMC's activities, including SIF strategies, and must ensure compliance and fair treatment of investors.
The custodian of a mutual fund scheme is responsible for:
Safekeeping securities and settling trades
Choosing which securities the fund manager should buy and sell for the portfolio
Selling units to investors
Fixing the scheme's TER
Custodians hold securities in safe custody, settle purchases and sales, and track corporate actions. Investment decisions remain with the AMC.
The Investment Management Agreement of a mutual fund is signed between:
Sponsor and investors, at the time of every new fund offer of a scheme
Trustees and the AMC
AMC and distributors
Custodian and SEBI
The IMA appoints the AMC to manage the fund's money and sets out its duties. It is executed between the trustees and the AMC.
Which entity maintains the record of unitholders and processes their transactions for most AMCs?
The sponsor of the mutual fund, through its own branch network
The custodian
The RTA
The statutory auditor
Registrar and transfer agents handle investor records, transaction processing, statements and many investor service requests on behalf of the AMC.
An AMC's board has 8 directors. Under SEBI norms, the minimum number who must be independent of the sponsor is:
6, plus the chairperson, in every case
None
SEBI requires at least 50% of an AMC's directors to be independent of the sponsor and associates. For the trustee board the requirement is two-thirds.
Under SEBI regulations, a mutual fund is constituted in the form of a:
Private limited company owned by the investors of all schemes
Partnership firm
Co-operative society
Trust
Indian mutual funds are set up as trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, with the sponsor as settlor, the trustees holding property for unitholders and the AMC as manager.

Legal and Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers regulations that apply to mutual funds and SIFs: investment restrictions, borrowing limits, advertisement rules, SIF-specific norms on minimum investment and distributor eligibility, and investor grievance redressal. Revise how SIFs must be branded separately, who may distribute them (NISM V-D certified distributors), the accredited investor exemption, the role of AMFI codes, and how complaints move from the AMC to SCORES and online dispute resolution. Expect scenario questions on what a distributor may or may not do.
questions: An investor's SIF holding falls below ₹10 lakh only because the market fell. Under SEBI's framework, this is treated as:
A passive breach, not requiring exit
A violation that requires the AMC to redeem all units immediately at the prevailing NAV
A reason to charge a penalty
Grounds to freeze the folio
The minimum investment is tested on investment amount. A fall in value due to market movement is a passive breach and does not force redemption.
Which body issues the certification that a distributor must pass before selling SIF strategies?
AMFI, through a separate SIF distributor licence that replaces the ARN
RBI
NISM
CDSL
NISM conducts the Series V-D certification for SIF distributors. Distributors also hold an ARN from AMFI, but the specific certification comes from NISM.
An AMC's SIF advertisement uses the same brand and look as its regular mutual fund schemes. Under SEBI norms this is:
Allowed, as long as the SIF has a separate fund manager
Allowed for accredited investors only
Required for brand consistency
Not allowed
SIFs must carry distinct branding so investors do not confuse them with regular mutual fund schemes that have lower minimums and different risks.
SEBI's power to regulate mutual funds and SIFs flows from the:
Banking Regulation Act, 1949
SEBI Act, 1992
Indian Contract Act, 1872, and the Indian Trusts Act read together
RBI Act, 1934
The SEBI Act empowers SEBI to regulate collective investment vehicles. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 and SIF circulars are issued under it.
A mutual fund scheme may borrow only to meet temporary liquidity needs. The maximum borrowing is:
50% of net assets, for up to one year, to buy additional securities
Unlimited, with trustee approval
20% of net assets, up to 6 months
10% of net assets for any purpose
Borrowing is allowed only for redemptions or IDCW payouts, up to 20% of net assets and for a maximum of six months. It cannot be used to leverage the portfolio.
A distributor tells a client that an SIF's long-short approach 'makes losses impossible'. This statement is:
Correct, since shorts offset all long positions under every market condition
Correct for hybrid strategies only
Acceptable if the client is wealthy
Misleading and a breach of conduct
Long-short strategies can still lose money, for example when both long and short positions move against the manager. Promising no losses is misrepresentation.
If an investor's grievance is not resolved by the AMC, the next escalation is usually:
Filing a police complaint against the distributor's branch office
SEBI's SCORES platform
The Banking Ombudsman
AMFI's board of directors
Investors first approach the AMC; if unresolved, they can file on SCORES. Disputes still pending can be taken to the online dispute resolution mechanism.
All schemes of a mutual fund together may not hold more than what share of the voting capital of any single company?
25% of the paid-up capital of each investee company
The 10% fund-level cap on voting rights prevents mutual funds from gaining control of investee companies and limits concentration.

Scheme Related Information.overview: This chapter covers the offer documents and disclosures for mutual funds and SIFs. For SIFs, the strategy-level document is the Investment Strategy Information Document (ISID), supported by statutory information about the fund house. Revise what the ISID contains (strategy, asset allocation, risk band, redemption frequency and notice period, loads), portfolio disclosure rules, the difference between the SID, SAI and KIM for regular schemes, and fundamental attributes that trigger an exit option.
questions: An investor wants to know how often an SIF strategy allows redemptions and what notice period applies. The best source is the:
Consolidated Account Statement issued by the depository for the previous month
ISID
AMC's balance sheet
Distributor's visiting card
Redemption frequency and notice period are strategy terms, set out in the Investment Strategy Information Document. They can differ across SIF strategies.
Why might an SIF strategy have a notice period for redemptions while most regular open-ended equity schemes do not?
Because SEBI bans redemptions from SIFs during the first three years after the launch
To earn extra fees from investors
Because SIF NAVs are declared yearly
To manage less liquid long-short positions
Long-short and concentrated strategies may need time to unwind positions in an orderly way. A notice period protects remaining investors from forced selling.
The document containing fund-house-level information common to all schemes, such as details of the sponsor and trustees, is the:
SAI
Key Information Memorandum given along with each application form
Factsheet
ISID
The Statement of Additional Information holds statutory details common to the fund house. Scheme or strategy-specific details are in the SID or ISID.
Which of these would be a change in a fundamental attribute requiring an exit option for existing investors?
Appointment of a new co-fund manager for the strategy alongside the existing one
Change in the AMC's head office address
Change in investment objective
Revision of the factsheet design
Investment objective, type of scheme and terms of issue are fundamental attributes. Changing them requires notice and an exit option at NAV without load.
The Key Information Memorandum (KIM) is best described as:
A detailed legal document containing the full trust deed and AMC agreements
A monthly portfolio statement
An audit report
An abridged SID that accompanies forms
The KIM summarises the key features of a scheme, such as objective, asset allocation, loads and risk, and must be provided with every application form.
A regular mutual fund scheme's riskometer must be reviewed:
Monthly
Only once at the time of the new fund offer, and never again
Every five years
Only when SEBI asks
Riskometers are evaluated monthly based on the portfolio, and changes are disclosed so investors know if the scheme's risk has changed.
Which of the following must be disclosed by an SIF strategy in its offer document?
The personal contact numbers of all the investors who have invested in the strategy
A guaranteed return
Its risk-band level
The fund manager's salary
The ISID must show the strategy's risk-band so investors can judge its risk. Investor details are confidential and returns cannot be guaranteed.
Portfolio disclosure for SIF strategies helps investors mainly to:
Trade the underlying stocks themselves on the same day at the scheme's cost price
Check holdings against the mandate
Avoid exit loads
Calculate their tax liability exactly
Periodic disclosure shows what the strategy actually holds, including derivative positions, so investors can confirm it follows its stated approach.

Fund Distribution and Channel Management.overview: This chapter covers how mutual funds and SIFs are distributed. Revise ARN and EUIN, NISM certification requirements (V-A for mutual funds, V-D additionally for SIFs), trail-only commission, direct versus regular plans, due diligence of distributors by AMCs, and the line between distribution and investment advice. For SIFs, focus on suitability: the high minimum ticket and complex strategies mean distributors must assess the investor's wealth, experience and understanding carefully before recommending.
questions: A mutual fund distributor wants to distribute SIF strategies. In addition to holding a valid ARN, the distributor must:
Register with RBI as an NBFC and maintain a minimum net worth
Become a SEBI-registered portfolio manager
Pass NISM Series V-D
Hold a CA qualification
SEBI requires distributors of SIF strategies to clear the NISM-Series-V-D certification, which tests knowledge of SIF strategies and derivatives, in addition to the regular MFD requirements.
A client with a total investable corpus of ₹12 lakh wants to put ₹10 lakh in a long-short SIF. The distributor's best response is to:
Point out the concentration risk
Process it immediately, since the minimum is met and the client has asked for it
Ask for ₹2 lakh more
Suggest borrowing to invest more
Meeting the minimum does not make a product suitable. Putting over 80% of savings in a complex strategy creates concentration risk; the distributor should assess suitability carefully.
Commission paid to mutual fund distributors under current SEBI rules is:
Paid fully upfront at the time of investment out of the AMC's own books
Trail-based only
Paid by SEBI
Deducted from investors' redemption
Upfront commissions are not allowed. Distributors receive trail commission out of the scheme's expenses for as long as the client stays invested.
Why do AMCs conduct due diligence on large distributors?
To fix the NAV of the schemes distributed by them on each business day
To decide the investor's tax rate
To appoint them as trustees
To ensure proper conduct and avoid mis-selling
AMCs review the processes and conduct of distributors that meet set thresholds, including suitability checks and handling of conflicts, to protect investors.
A distributor wants to advise clients for a fee and also earn commission on the same clients. Under SEBI norms:
Advice and distribution must be segregated
Both can be done freely for the same client by the same individual
Only fee income is taxable
AMFI must approve each client
SEBI requires a clear separation between advisory (fee from client) and distribution (commission from AMC) to avoid conflicts. The same person cannot do both for the same client.
An investor who wants to invest in an SIF through a distributor will be allotted units of the:
Direct plan, because SIFs have only one plan for all investors
Regular plan
Institutional plan
Segregated plan
Investments through distributors go into the regular plan, whose expenses include distributor commission. Investments without a distributor go into the direct plan.
Which unique code identifies the specific employee of a distributing entity who dealt with the investor?
ARN of the AMC's branch office where the form is submitted
PAN of the distributor
ISIN of the scheme
EUIN
The EUIN (Employee Unique Identification Number) tracks which employee or relationship manager interacted with the investor, improving accountability for advice.
Which practice is acceptable for a mutual fund distributor?
Promising guaranteed returns on long-short strategies to attract high net worth clients
Collecting investor cheques in the distributor's own name
Disclosing commissions received
Signing forms on clients' behalf
Distributors must disclose commissions for schemes they recommend. Promising returns, collecting money in their own name or signing for clients are prohibited.

NAV, TER and Pricing of Units.overview: This chapter covers how NAV is calculated, how expenses are charged through the Total Expense Ratio, and the price at which units are bought and sold. Revise the NAV formula, daily expense accrual, slab-wise TER limits, exit loads, valuation of securities including derivatives used in long-short strategies, segregated portfolios after a credit event, and how IDCW affects NAV. For SIFs, understand that short derivative positions are marked to market daily and flow into NAV. Practise NAV and redemption calculations.
questions: A long-short strategy has long holdings worth ₹520 crore, a short futures position with a mark-to-market loss of ₹8 crore, cash of ₹15 crore and other liabilities of ₹7 crore. With 50 crore units, the NAV is:
₹10.70, since futures losses are booked only when the position is finally closed
Net assets = 520 − 8 + 15 − 7 = ₹520 crore. NAV = 520 / 50 = ₹10.40. Daily mark-to-market losses on derivatives reduce NAV immediately; ignoring the ₹8 crore loss gives ₹10.56.
Which expense must be borne by the AMC rather than charged to the scheme?
Custodian fees charged for safekeeping of the scheme's securities within the limit
Expenses above the TER limit
Registrar fees
Audit fees
Only permitted expenses up to SEBI's TER limits can be charged to a scheme. Anything beyond the limit is borne by the AMC, its sponsor or trustees.
An investor redeems 2,000 units at an NAV of ₹45 with an exit load of 0.5%. The amount paid before tax is:
₹90,450, because the exit load is added to the NAV paid to the investor
Redemption price = 45 × (1 − 0.005) = ₹44.775. Proceeds = 2,000 × 44.775 = ₹89,550. ₹89,100 applies a 1% load instead.
A segregated portfolio is created in a debt scheme when:
A held security suffers a credit event
The scheme's AUM falls below ₹100 crore during any quarter of the financial year
The fund manager resigns
Interest rates rise sharply
Segregation (side-pocketing) separates a downgraded or defaulted security from the main portfolio so new and redeeming investors are treated fairly, and existing investors keep any later recovery.
Daily accrual of expenses means that:
Expenses are charged to investors once a year as a separate bill payable by cheque
NAV is published net of expenses
Expenses are deducted from SIP instalments only
Expenses are recovered from distributors
Expenses are accrued every day within the TER, so each published NAV already reflects them. Investors do not pay a separate bill.
A scheme declares an IDCW of ₹2 per unit when its cum-IDCW NAV is ₹32. Ignoring market movement, the ex-IDCW NAV is:
₹32, as IDCW is paid out of the AMC's own profits and not from the NAV
IDCW is paid out of the scheme's assets, so NAV falls by the amount paid: 32 − 2 = ₹30. The investor's total value (NAV plus cash) is unchanged.
Exit load collected by a scheme is:
Credited back to the scheme
Retained by the distributor as an additional commission for the investor's account
Paid to SEBI
Kept by the AMC as profit
Exit load, net of GST, is credited to the scheme, so it benefits remaining investors and discourages short-term flows that impose costs on them.
How are exchange-traded futures held by a scheme valued for NAV purposes?
At the original contract price until expiry, without any daily adjustment
At the face value of the underlying
At the fund manager's estimate
At the exchange settlement price
Exchange-traded derivatives are valued at the daily settlement or closing price published by the exchange, so gains and losses are reflected in NAV every day.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers taxation of mutual fund and SIF investments in India. Revise how a scheme is classified for tax (equity-oriented with at least 65% domestic equity, specified debt-oriented schemes, and others), holding periods, current capital gains rates, IDCW taxation and TDS, set-off and carry-forward of losses, and the treatment of switches. For long-short SIF strategies, note that classification depends on the actual equity exposure as defined by tax law. Rates change with Budgets, so confirm current figures before the exam.
questions: An SIF strategy keeps at least 65% of its assets in domestic listed equity, including hedged positions as permitted by tax rules. For tax purposes it would be treated as:
Equity-oriented
A specified debt-oriented fund taxed at slab rates, irrespective of holding period
A business trust
An exempt instrument
Tax treatment follows the portfolio composition. A fund meeting the 65% domestic equity threshold is equity-oriented, so equity capital gains rates and the 12-month holding period apply.
Equity-oriented fund units held for 10 months are sold at a gain of ₹80,000. Ignoring cess, the tax on this gain is:
₹10,000, since gains below ₹1.25 lakh are taxed at the long-term rate
Nil
Units held for 12 months or less give short-term gains, taxed at 20% for equity-oriented funds. 20% of ₹80,000 = ₹16,000. The ₹1.25 lakh exemption applies only to long-term gains.
A long-term capital loss on mutual fund units that cannot be set off this year can be carried forward for up to:
4 assessment years, and only against business income of those years
1 year
Indefinitely
8 assessment years
Capital losses can be carried forward for eight assessment years, provided the return is filed on time. Long-term losses can only be set off against long-term gains.
A resident investor receives IDCW from a mutual fund. Which statement is correct?
It is exempt because the fund has already paid dividend distribution tax on it
It is taxed at the investor's slab rate
It is taxed at 12.5% flat
It is taxed only on redemption
Dividend distribution tax was abolished in 2020. IDCW is now taxed in the investor's hands at slab rates, with TDS above the prescribed threshold.
An investor switches units from an equity long-short SIF strategy to a debt strategy of the same AMC. For tax purposes, this is:
Exempt, since the AMC and the investor remain the same
Taxable only if exit load is charged
A taxable transfer
Treated as a gift
A switch is a redemption from one scheme or strategy and a purchase in another, so any capital gain on the units switched out is taxable.
Securities Transaction Tax applies on redemption of units of:
Debt-oriented schemes and liquid funds, at the same rate as equity schemes
All schemes equally
Gold ETFs only
Equity-oriented schemes
STT is levied on redemption of units of equity-oriented funds, at a small rate. Redemption of debt schemes does not attract STT.
For equity units acquired before 1 February 2018, grandfathering means that:
All gains on those units are fully exempt from tax forever, whenever they are sold
Gains till 31 Jan 2018 are protected
Indexation applies from 2001
The units are taxed at slab rates
Cost is stepped up to the fair market value on 31 January 2018 (subject to limits), so gains accrued up to that date are not taxed under the long-term equity regime.
A non-resident investor redeems equity fund units at a gain. Tax on the gain is generally:
Deducted at source by the fund
Collected only when the investor files a return in the country of residence
Never payable in India
Paid by the distributor
For non-residents, the mutual fund deducts tax at source on capital gains at the applicable rates before paying redemption proceeds, subject to any treaty benefit claimed.

Investor Services.overview: This chapter covers the investor's journey: KYC, applying for units, cut-off times and applicable NAV, systematic plans, redemptions, statements, nomination and transmission. For SIFs, revise how the minimum investment is checked at PAN level across strategies of an AMC, how systematic plans work once the threshold is met, and how redemption frequency and notice periods apply. For regular schemes, know cut-off rules, payment timelines and processes for minors, NRIs and change of details.
questions: An investor already holds ₹12 lakh across SIF strategies of an AMC and wants to invest ₹1 lakh in another strategy of the same AMC. Under the minimum investment rule:
Not allowed, since every new strategy needs a separate ₹10 lakh investment
This is allowed
Allowed only through a lumpsum of ₹5 lakh
Allowed only for accredited investors
The ₹10 lakh minimum is checked at the investor's PAN level across all SIF strategies of the AMC. Having met it, the investor can add smaller amounts.
For an equity scheme, a purchase application received at 2:45 pm on Wednesday, with funds reaching the scheme's account at 4 pm the same day, gets:
Wednesday's NAV, because the application itself was received before the 3 pm cut-off
Tuesday's NAV
Friday's NAV
Thursday's NAV
For equity schemes, the applicable NAV depends on when funds are available for use. Funds realised after the 3 pm cut-off get the next business day's NAV.
Which document is mandatory for a resident individual's KYC for mutual fund investments above micro limits?
PAN
Passport, as the only acceptable identity and address proof for KYC
Voter ID only
Driving licence only
PAN is mandatory for all mutual fund investments except PAN-exempt micro investments. Other documents serve as proof of address.
SIP, STP and SWP facilities in SIF strategies can be used by an investor:
Freely from the first instalment, without any minimum amount at all
Only in debt strategies
After the minimum is met
Never
SIFs allow systematic plans, but the investor must first meet the ₹10 lakh threshold at PAN level (unless exempt as an accredited investor).
When the sole holder of a folio dies without a nominee, the legal heir will typically need to submit:
Only a self-attested copy of the heir's PAN and nothing else
A fresh application for allotment
A redemption request signed by a distributor
Legal documents proving succession
Without a nominee, the AMC needs documents such as a succession certificate, probate, or indemnity and NOCs (based on value) to establish the claimant's right.
A Consolidated Account Statement for a demat account holder who also holds mutual fund units in statement form is generated by:
The depositories
The investor's bank, along with the monthly savings bank statement
SEBI
Each distributor separately
Where the investor has a demat account, the depositories send a single CAS covering demat holdings and mutual fund folios linked through PAN.
An NRI wants returns on a mutual fund investment to be fully repatriable. The investment should be funded from:
An NRO account, which is always fully repatriable without limits
A resident savings account
An NRE account
Cash
NRE account funds and proceeds are freely repatriable. NRO funds are generally non-repatriable, subject to permitted remittance limits.
Redemption proceeds of most open-ended schemes must be transferred to investors within:
10 working days from the end of the month in which the request is made
3 working days
1 month
1 working day
SEBI requires redemption proceeds to be paid within three working days for most schemes, with specified exceptions for schemes facing special circumstances.

Risk, Return and Performance of Funds.overview: This chapter explains how to measure risk and return for mutual funds and long-short strategies. Revise standard deviation, beta, downside deviation and drawdown, and risk-adjusted measures such as Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino and alpha. For long-short strategies, understand net and gross exposure, how a lower net exposure reduces market sensitivity, and the risk that both long and short sides lose together. Also cover interest rate, credit and liquidity risk in debt portfolios. Expect calculations on Sharpe, Treynor and exposure.
questions: A long-short strategy is 90% long and 30% short. Its net market exposure is:
120%, being the total of the long and the short positions added together
Net exposure = long − short = 90% − 30% = 60%. Gross exposure (long + short) is 120%, which indicates total positions rather than market sensitivity.
Compared with a fully invested long-only equity fund, a long-short fund with lower net exposure will typically have:
Lower sensitivity to market moves
Higher beta and larger swings than the market in both directions
No risk of any loss
Zero tracking error
Lower net exposure means less market (beta) risk. Losses are still possible if stock selection on either side goes wrong.
Fund P returned 16% with standard deviation 20%; Fund Q returned 12% with standard deviation 10%. The risk-free rate is 6%. Which has the better Sharpe ratio?
Fund P, because it delivered the higher absolute return over the year
Fund Q
Both are equal
Cannot be computed
Sharpe P = (16 − 6) / 20 = 0.50. Sharpe Q = (12 − 6) / 10 = 0.60. Fund Q earns more excess return per unit of total risk.
A long-short manager buys stock A and shorts stock B. The market rises, A falls and B rises. The likely result is:
Gains on both sides, since a long-short strategy is hedged against all market moves
Gain on A only
No change in NAV
Losses on both sides
The long position in A loses as A falls, and the short in B loses as B rises. Long-short strategies can lose on both legs when stock selection is wrong.
Which risk measure focuses only on returns below a minimum acceptable level?
Downside deviation
Standard deviation, which treats upside and downside moves in the same way
Beta
R-squared
Downside deviation measures volatility of returns below a target. It is used in the Sortino ratio, which penalises only harmful volatility.
A debt portfolio has a modified duration of 3. If yields rise by 0.5%, its value will change by approximately:
+1.5%, as rising yields increase the coupon income of the portfolio
Price change ≈ −modified duration × change in yield = −3 × 0.5% = −1.5%. Prices fall when yields rise.
A fund holding thinly traded securities faces heavy redemptions. The danger it faces is best described as:
Sponsor risk, i.e. the sponsor being unable to support the AMC financially
Interest rate risk
Tracking risk
Liquidity risk
Illiquid holdings may have to be sold at a discount to meet redemptions, which hurts remaining investors. Notice periods in SIFs help manage this.
A fund's beta is 0.6 relative to Nifty. If Nifty falls 10%, the fund is expected to fall about:
16%, since beta adds to the market fall instead of scaling it
Expected move = beta × market move = 0.6 × −10% = −6%. A beta below 1 indicates lower sensitivity to market movements.

Mutual Fund Scheme Performance.overview: This chapter covers how to evaluate scheme and strategy performance. Revise two-tier benchmarking, the use of total return indices, rolling versus point-to-point returns, CAGR and XIRR, tracking error and information ratio, and why peer comparison must stay within the same category or strategy type. For long-short SIFs, consider performance relative to an appropriate benchmark and on a risk-adjusted basis, including behaviour in falling markets. Practise CAGR and information ratio calculations.
questions: For investments made at different dates and amounts, such as a SIP, the most appropriate return measure is:
Simple absolute return calculated from the first instalment date to today
Point-to-point CAGR
Average NAV
XIRR
XIRR accounts for the timing and size of each cash flow, giving an annualised return for irregular or periodic investments like SIPs.
A scheme beat its benchmark by an average 1.5% a year with a tracking error of 5%. Its information ratio is:
3.33, being the tracking error divided by the excess return earned
Information ratio = excess return / tracking error = 1.5 / 5 = 0.30. It measures how consistently a manager adds value relative to the benchmark.
Why should a long-short SIF be judged partly on its behaviour in falling markets?
Because SEBI requires SIFs to show positive returns in every quarter
Because SIF NAVs do not fall
Its aim is to limit downside
Because falling markets have no effect on long-only funds
A key promise of long-short strategies is better downside management through short positions. Checking drawdowns in falling markets tests whether this works.
₹10 lakh invested grew to ₹16 lakh in 4 years. The CAGR is closest to:
15.0%, being the 60% gain spread equally over the four years
CAGR = (16/10)^(1/4) − 1 ≈ 12.47%. Dividing the 60% absolute gain by four years gives 15%, which ignores compounding.
Under two-tier benchmarking, the second-tier benchmark of a scheme:
Must always be the Nifty 50 Price Return Index, for every category
Reflects the scheme's own style
Is chosen by the investor
Applies only to debt schemes
The first tier reflects the category; the second tier is chosen by the AMC to better match the specific scheme's investment style or strategy.
Equity scheme returns are compared with a Total Return Index rather than a price index because:
TRI excludes dividends, making the comparison stricter for the fund
Price indices are not published
TRI includes dividends
TRI is calculated by the AMC
Funds receive dividends and include them in NAV, so the fair comparison is with a TRI, which assumes dividends are reinvested.
When comparing SIF strategies, a fair comparison would be between:
Strategies of the same type
An equity long-short SIF and a liquid fund, using one-year returns only
An SIF and a bank FD
Any two SIFs regardless of type
Strategy types differ in risk and objective. Like-for-like comparison within the same strategy type, and against an appropriate benchmark, is meaningful.
A high tracking error in an index fund indicates that:
The fund has beaten the index by a large margin in every single period
The fund has low expenses
The index is volatile
Returns deviate a lot from the index
Tracking error is the variability of the gap between fund and index returns. A passive fund should keep it low; a high figure points to poor replication.

Mutual Fund Scheme Selection.overview: This chapter is about matching products to investors. Revise how goals, horizon, risk profile, liquidity needs and tax status guide the choice among mutual fund categories and SIF strategies. For SIFs, suitability is central: they need a ₹10 lakh minimum, may have restricted redemption frequency, and use derivatives and short positions. Distributors must judge whether the investor has adequate wealth, experience and understanding. Also cover choosing between active and passive, and growth versus IDCW options.
questions: Which investor is the most suitable for an equity long-short SIF?
A wealthy, experienced investor with a long horizon
A first-time investor who needs all of the money back within six months
A retiree relying on the corpus for monthly expenses
A student investing pocket money
SIFs suit investors who can meet the minimum, understand derivative-based strategies, can bear losses and do not need quick access to the money.
An investor who wants daily liquidity with very low risk should prefer:
A sector rotation long-short SIF with a weekly redemption window and notice period
A small cap fund
A liquid or overnight fund
A credit risk fund
Liquid and overnight funds offer daily redemption and low volatility. SIFs may restrict redemptions and carry higher risk.
An investor wants equity exposure with lower downside than a long-only fund, can invest ₹25 lakh, and has a 5-year horizon. A reasonable option to consider is:
An overnight fund, as it gives equity returns with no downside
A gilt fund with 10-year maturity
A sectoral long-only fund
