Market Participants in the Securities Ma.overview: This chapter describes the participants in the securities market: investors (retail, HNI, institutional, FPIs, NRIs), issuers, stock brokers, authorised persons, depository participants, custodians, clearing members, merchant bankers, RTAs, credit rating agencies and others, along with the market infrastructure institutions. Revise the role of each, how investors are categorised in IPOs, and which regulator or body governs each participant.
questions: In a public issue, an individual investor applying for shares worth up to ₹2 lakh is classified as a:
Non-institutional investor
Qualified institutional buyer
Retail individual investor
Anchor investor
Individuals applying for up to ₹2 lakh are retail individual investors. Applications above ₹2 lakh by individuals fall in the non-institutional category.
Which intermediary assigns ratings to debt instruments based on the issuer's ability to repay?
A credit rating agency
A merchant banker
A custodian
A depository
Credit rating agencies, registered with SEBI, assess the creditworthiness of issuers and their debt instruments. Ratings help investors judge default risk.
The intermediary that manages a public issue, prepares the offer document and conducts due diligence is the:
Registrar to the issue
Merchant banker
Stock broker
Clearing bank
Merchant bankers (book running lead managers) handle the issue process, due diligence and offer document. The registrar processes applications and allotments.
Which participant settles funds of clearing members with the clearing corporation?
Credit rating agency
Authorised person
Investment adviser
Clearing bank
Clearing banks maintain settlement accounts of clearing members and move funds for pay-in and pay-out as instructed by the clearing corporation.
An anchor investor in an IPO is:
A QIB allotted shares before the issue opens
Any retail investor who bids on the first day of the issue
The promoter of the company
A stock exchange
Anchor investors are QIBs who are allotted shares a day before the issue opens to the public, subject to lock-in, which helps signal institutional demand.
Which of these is NOT a market infrastructure institution?
A stock exchange
A merchant banker
A clearing corporation
A depository
MIIs are stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories. Merchant bankers are intermediaries registered with SEBI.
A stock broker's agent who deals with clients and is approved by the exchange is called a(n):
Sub-custodian
Sponsor
Trustee
Authorised person
Authorised persons act on behalf of a broker and must be approved by the exchange. Investors' contracts remain with the stock broker.
A foreign pension fund investing in Indian listed shares would participate as a(n):
Authorised person
Domestic institutional investor
Foreign portfolio investor
Retail individual investor
Foreign institutional investors register with SEBI (through DDPs) as FPIs to invest in Indian listed securities.

Introduction to Securities Broking Opera.overview: This chapter covers how a broking firm operates: front, middle and back office functions; client onboarding and KYC; order types and order management; the trade life cycle from order to settlement; contract notes; and client funds handling. Revise order types (market, limit, stop-loss, IOC, day orders), what a contract note contains and when it must be issued, client-level segregation, and the role of unique client codes. Questions are practical and scenario-based.
questions: A client wants an order that stays active only until the end of the trading day if not executed. This is a:
Immediate or cancel order
Good till cancelled order
Market order
Day order
A day order is valid only for the trading day; unexecuted quantity is cancelled at the close. An IOC must execute immediately or be cancelled.
A contract note issued by a broker must contain:
The client's net worth
Trade details and charges
The client's tax computation
The broker's balance sheet
Contract notes show trade time, price, quantity, brokerage, taxes and other levies. They are legal records of the trade and must be issued within 24 hours.
A client places a market order to buy 100 shares. The order will:
Execute only at the previous close
Wait until a limit price is reached
Execute at the best available price
Be cancelled if not executed in 10 minutes
A market order executes immediately against the best available sell orders, giving certainty of execution but not of price.
Which unit in a broking firm usually handles settlement of funds and securities with the clearing corporation?
Back office
Front office
Research desk
Marketing team
The back office handles post-trade work: settlement, reconciliation, client ledgers and statutory reporting. The front office takes orders.
Every order placed on the exchange must be tagged with the client's:
Bank branch code
Unique Client Code
ISIN
Contract note number
The UCC links each order to a registered client with KYC details, enabling exchange surveillance and client-level monitoring.
A client wants to buy only if the price falls to ₹420 or below. The client should place a:
Market buy order
Stop-loss sell order at ₹420
Limit buy order at ₹420
IOC sell order
A limit buy order executes only at the specified price or lower. A market order would buy at the current price, above ₹420.
Funds received from clients must be:
Kept in client bank accounts, segregated
Used for the broker's proprietary trades
Deposited in the broker's own savings account
Lent to other clients
Client funds must be kept in designated client bank accounts and used only for that client's obligations, under SEBI's segregation rules.
Before executing trades for a new client, a broker must ensure:
The client has traded elsewhere before
The client has a minimum income of ₹10 lakh
The client has bought an IPO
KYC and client registration are complete
KYC, PAN verification and client registration documentation are prerequisites for trading. No minimum income or prior trading history is required.

Risk Management.overview: This chapter explains how exchanges, clearing corporations and brokers control risk. Revise the margin system in the cash segment (VaR margin, extreme loss margin, mark-to-market), upfront and peak margin collection, penalties for short collection, position and concentration limits, the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund, and broker-level risk controls such as square-off policies. Practise MTM and margin calculations and understand what each type of margin protects against.
questions: A client sells 200 shares at ₹750. The day's closing price is ₹765. The mark-to-market loss is:
No loss, since the sale is complete
The short position loses when price rises: 200 × (765 − 750) = ₹3,000. MTM is computed against the closing price until settlement.
Peak margin requirements mean that brokers must ensure:
Margins are checked only at end of day
Clients pay margin after settlement
Margins cover intraday peak positions
No margin applies to intraday trades
Clearing corporations take multiple intraday snapshots and check collected margin against the peak requirement, so clients cannot take positions without adequate margin.
Upfront margin in the cash segment must be collected from clients:
Within seven days of the trade
Only on loss-making trades
At the end of the month
Before trading
SEBI requires brokers to collect VaR and ELM margins upfront from clients before trades are executed, reducing default risk.
Concentration limits imposed by a broker on a single client mainly reduce:
Brokerage revenue earned from the client
Exposure to one client or stock
Number of trades
Exchange fees
Concentration limits prevent a large part of the broker's risk being tied to one client or one illiquid stock, which could cause big losses on default.
A broker collects less margin than required for a client's position. The consequence is that:
The trade is automatically cancelled
The client gets a refund
A penalty for short collection is levied
SEBI pays the shortfall
Clearing corporations levy penalties on short collection of margins, which brokers cannot pass on in a manner violating norms; the aim is to enforce upfront margin discipline.
VaR margin is typically computed to cover potential losses on a position over:
The entire remaining life of the company
Ten years of history
Only the next minute
A short period at a high confidence level
VaR estimates the maximum likely loss over a short horizon (usually a day or two) at a high confidence level such as 99%.
A client's ledger shows an unpaid debit and the stock is falling. A broker's risk policy would typically allow it to:
Ignore it till the client pays
Square off positions after notice
Use another client's securities
Charge interest only
Brokers can liquidate positions as per their disclosed risk management policy to recover dues and limit further losses.
The Core SGF of a clearing corporation is used:
To meet settlement when a member defaults
To pay dividends to investors of listed companies
To fund IPOs
To pay exchange salaries
The Core Settlement Guarantee Fund guarantees completion of settlement if a clearing member defaults, after using the defaulter's own resources.

Clearing Process.overview: This chapter explains clearing: determining who owes what after trading. Revise novation by the clearing corporation, multilateral netting, the roles of clearing members, custodians and clearing banks, confirmation of institutional trades, the interface with depositories, and the settlement calendar. Understand the difference between clearing (computing obligations) and settlement (actual exchange of funds and securities), and practise simple netting examples.
questions: A broker's clients buy 1,000 shares and sell 700 shares of the same stock in the same settlement. The broker's net securities obligation is to:
Deliver 300 shares
Receive 300 shares
Receive 1,700 shares
Deliver 1,000 shares
Netting offsets buys and sells: 1,000 bought − 700 sold = net receipt of 300 shares. Netting reduces the volume of securities and funds that must move.
Novation in clearing means that:
Trades are cancelled if prices move by more than the circuit limit
Brokers settle directly with each other
SEBI guarantees each trade
The clearing corporation becomes counterparty to both sides
With novation, the clearing corporation interposes itself between buyer and seller, so each party's counterparty risk is on the clearing corporation.
Institutional trades executed by a broker for a custodian's client become final only after:
The custodian confirms them
The issuer approves them
SEBI approves them
The client pays tax
Trades with a custodial participant code must be confirmed by the custodian; on confirmation, settlement responsibility moves to the custodian's clearing member.
The difference between clearing and settlement is that clearing:
Moves securities; settlement computes obligations
Happens after settlement
Determines obligations; settlement discharges them
Is done by depositories only
Clearing works out each member's net funds and securities obligations. Settlement is the actual pay-in and pay-out of those funds and securities.
Clearing members' fund obligations are settled through:
Cash deposits at the exchange
Cheques to SEBI
The RTA's account
Designated clearing banks
Each clearing member maintains a settlement account with a clearing bank, which is debited or credited as instructed by the clearing corporation.
A trader buys and sells the same quantity of a stock on the same day in the cash segment. Under netting, the delivery obligation is:
Nil, only price difference settled
Full delivery of both legs
Delivery of the bought shares
Settled next month
Intraday buy and sell of equal quantity net to zero shares; only the money difference (profit or loss) is settled.
Which entity provides clearing corporations with the details of trades executed?
The depository
The RTA
The stock exchange
The clearing bank
Exchanges pass trade data to the clearing corporation, which computes obligations and coordinates with depositories and clearing banks for settlement.
Why does netting reduce settlement risk?
It eliminates price risk for both buyers and sellers
Fewer funds and securities need to move
It guarantees profits
It removes the need for margins
By offsetting buys and sells, netting lowers the gross amount to be settled, reducing liquidity needs and the impact of any single failure.

Settlement Process.overview: This chapter covers settlement of trades under the T+1 cycle (and the optional T+0 framework): pay-in and pay-out timelines, direct pay-out to clients, handling of short deliveries through auction and close-out, bad deliveries, settlement holidays, and how corporate actions affect open positions. Practise working out settlement dates around weekends and holidays, and understand who bears the cost of a failed delivery.
questions: A trade is executed on Wednesday. Thursday is a settlement holiday. Under T+1, settlement happens on:
Thursday
Wednesday
Friday
Monday
T+1 counts working days for settlement. With Thursday a settlement holiday, the next working day, Friday, is the settlement day.
If a security cannot be bought in the auction after a short delivery, the trade is:
Closed out at a prescribed price
Cancelled with no payment to either party
Kept open indefinitely
Settled by SEBI
When an auction fails, the buyer is compensated through close-out at a price set by the clearing corporation's rules, usually higher than the trade price.
The cost of an auction resulting from a seller's short delivery is borne by:
The buyer
The defaulting seller
The exchange
SEBI
The seller who failed to deliver bears the auction price difference and penalties, discouraging short sales without delivery in the cash segment.
Under the optional T+0 settlement cycle, trades are settled:
One day later
Two days later
At month end
On the same day
SEBI's optional T+0 (beta) framework lets a limited set of stocks settle on the trade day itself, alongside the regular T+1 cycle.
A client sells shares on Monday under T+1. The broker transfers the sale proceeds to the client:
After pay-out on Tuesday
Before the sale on Monday
Next month
Only on request after a year
Funds pay-out happens on settlement day (Tuesday); the broker then credits the client, subject to SEBI's timelines for releasing client funds.
Funds pay-in for a clearing member must be made:
Any time within a week
By the settlement-day pay-in time
Only after pay-out
On the trade date before market opens
Clearing members must ensure funds are available in their clearing bank account by the pay-in deadline on settlement day so pay-out can proceed.
When a company declares a stock split, open stock futures positions are:
Closed out by the exchange at the last traded price
Left unchanged
Converted into options
Adjusted in lot size and price
Exchanges adjust derivative contracts for corporate actions like splits and bonuses, changing lot size and price so the position's value is preserved.
Which statement about settlement of trades in the cash segment is correct?
Each trade settles separately on a gross basis
Settlement depends on client consent
Obligations are settled on a net basis
Settlement is optional
Clearing corporations net each member's buys and sells across trades in a settlement, and only net obligations are settled.

Investor Grievances and Arbitration.overview: This chapter covers how investors can resolve complaints against brokers, listed companies and other intermediaries. Revise the escalation path (intermediary, exchange, SCORES), timelines for resolution, the Online Dispute Resolution mechanism with conciliation and arbitration, the Investor Protection Fund and its use when a broker defaults, and what is not a valid ground for complaint. Questions are mostly conceptual and scenario-based.
questions: Under SEBI's ODR mechanism, a dispute is first attempted to be resolved through:
A civil court hearing
Direct arbitration only
A complaint to RBI
Online conciliation
The ODR process starts with online conciliation. If that fails, the matter can proceed to online arbitration through empanelled ODR institutions.
The Investor Protection Fund of a stock exchange pays claims when:
Share prices fall
A broker is declared a defaulter
A company skips a dividend
An IPO is undersubscribed
IPF compensates eligible investor claims against defaulting brokers up to specified limits; it does not cover investment losses due to market movement.
Four clients write to their broker. Whose grievance is a genuine service deficiency by the broker?
Loss on a stock bought on own decision
The market fell after purchase
Non-receipt of funds after a sale
A company cut its dividend
Failure to pay out sale proceeds is a service deficiency. Market losses on one's own decisions are not grounds for complaint.
An investor wants to complain online against a listed company and track the complaint. The platform is:
SCORES
UPI
e-voting
MF Utility
SCORES is SEBI's online grievance redress system for listed companies and intermediaries, with tracking of status and escalation.
Arbitration awards under the exchange or ODR mechanism are:
Merely advisory and can be ignored by the broker
Binding, subject to legal challenge
Valid only if SEBI signs
Applicable only to brokers
Arbitral awards are binding on parties, subject to challenge under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. They provide a faster route than civil courts.
A client finds unauthorised trades in her account. Her first step should be to:
Ignore it if the amount involved is small
Sell all holdings
Raise it with the broker in writing
Close her bank account
Investors should promptly report unauthorised trades to the broker in writing; if not resolved, escalate to the exchange or SCORES and then ODR.
Exchanges maintain a mechanism to resolve complaints between investors and listed companies or brokers mainly because:
They supervise their members and listed companies
They guarantee investment returns
They are owned by investors
They set income tax rates
Exchanges have regulatory responsibilities over members and listed companies, so they handle investor complaints and can take action against them.
Which of these is NOT covered by the Investor Protection Fund?
Securities due from a defaulting broker
Funds due from a defaulting broker
Eligible claims after default
Losses from speculative trades
IPF covers eligible claims for funds and securities due from a defaulting broker. It does not compensate losses on trades made by the investor.

Other Services Provided by Brokers.overview: This chapter covers services brokers offer beyond basic trading: margin trading facility, securities lending and borrowing, portfolio management, mutual fund distribution through exchange platforms, research, internet and algorithmic trading, and depository services. Revise eligibility and permissions needed, how MTF works and its risks, the minimum investment for PMS, SLB mechanics, and safeguards for internet and algorithmic trading.
questions: Under Securities Lending and Borrowing (SLB), a lender of shares earns:
A lending fee
The full market gain
Voting rights only
A guaranteed dividend
The lender earns a lending fee while lending shares through the SLB platform. The borrower uses the shares, often to cover short sales or settlement needs.
In the Margin Trading Facility, the securities bought by the client are:
Transferred to the broker's own account
Rematerialised
Pledged in favour of the broker
Kept with SEBI
MTF positions are held in the client's account and pledged to the broker as collateral for the funding provided.
A broker offering algorithmic trading to clients must:
Allow unlimited orders per second
Avoid audits
Hide the algos from the exchange
Get exchange approval for the algos
Algorithmic trading requires exchange approval, risk controls and audits so that algorithms do not disrupt markets or cause runaway orders.
Which service requires a broker to register separately with SEBI?
Order placement for cash market trades
Portfolio management
Issuing contract notes
Providing a trading app
Portfolio management requires separate SEBI registration as a portfolio manager. The other activities are part of normal broking operations.
A broker's research report recommending stocks is covered by:
RBI's KYC Master Directions for banks
IRDAI's guidelines
SEBI Research Analyst Regulations
The Depositories Act
Research reports must comply with SEBI's Research Analyst Regulations, including disclosures on conflicts of interest and holdings.
A key risk for a client using MTF is that:
Brokerage is fully waived
Dividends are lost
Shares cannot be sold later
Leverage magnifies losses
Borrowed money magnifies gains and losses. A fall in prices can trigger margin calls and forced sale of pledged shares.
A broker offering demat services to clients must also be registered as a:
Merchant banker
Depository Participant
Mutual fund
Credit rating agency
Opening and maintaining demat accounts requires DP registration with SEBI through a depository.
Mutual fund orders placed by a broker on an exchange platform are settled through:
The clearing corporation
The AMC's sponsor
The trustee
RBI
Exchange mutual fund platforms route orders to AMCs/RTAs, with funds and units settled through the clearing corporation.

Indian Economy & Indian Financial System.overview: This paper covers the structure of the Indian economy and the financial system that supports it. Revise national income concepts (nominal and real GDP, deflator), fiscal indicators (fiscal, revenue and primary deficits), monetary policy tools and the liquidity adjustment framework including the SDF and MSF, the balance of payments, financial inclusion schemes, and the regulators of banking, securities, insurance, pensions and commodity markets. Practise simple calculations on growth, deficits and money multipliers.
questions: Nominal GDP grew by 11% in a year while the GDP deflator rose by 4%. Real GDP growth is closest to:
Real growth = (1.11 / 1.04) − 1 ≈ 6.7%. Simply subtracting gives 7%, a rough approximation. The deflator strips out price changes from nominal GDP.
Under RBI's liquidity adjustment framework, the floor of the policy rate corridor is the:
Marginal Standing Facility rate
Bank Rate
Cash Reserve Ratio
Standing Deposit Facility rate
Since 2022 the SDF, which absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral, forms the floor of the corridor, while the MSF rate forms the ceiling around the repo rate.
The government's fiscal deficit is ₹16 lakh crore and interest payments are ₹11 lakh crore. The primary deficit is:
₹5 lakh crore
₹27 lakh crore
₹11 lakh crore
₹16 lakh crore
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 16 − 11 = ₹5 lakh crore. It shows borrowing needed for spending other than past debt servicing.
Remittances sent home by Indians working abroad are recorded in India's balance of payments under the:
Capital account, as foreign direct investment
Financial account, as portfolio flows
Current account
Errors and omissions
Private transfers such as remittances are part of invisibles in the current account. FDI and portfolio flows belong to the capital/financial account.
If RBI lowers the policy repo rate, the most likely immediate effect is:
A rise in banks' cost of funds
An increase in the CRR
Higher yields on government bonds
Lower borrowing costs in the economy
A repo cut lowers the cost at which banks borrow from RBI, which typically passes into lower lending and deposit rates and lower bond yields.
Which regulator oversees commodity derivatives exchanges in India?
SEBI
Forward Markets Commission
Reserve Bank of India
Ministry of Consumer Affairs
The Forward Markets Commission was merged with SEBI in 2015, and SEBI now regulates commodity derivatives exchanges and brokers.
Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana is primarily aimed at:
Providing crop insurance to farmers
Funding large infrastructure projects
Universal access to basic bank accounts
Recapitalising public sector banks
PMJDY aims at financial inclusion by giving every household a basic savings account with RuPay card and access to insurance and credit facilities.
In a simplified model where banks keep only the CRR of 4% as reserves, the maximum money multiplier is:
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio = 1 / 0.04 = 25. In practice it is lower because of currency held by the public and excess reserves.

Principles & Practices of Banking.overview: This paper covers the legal and operational foundations of banking. Revise banker–customer relationships for different services, negotiable instruments (crossings, paying and collecting banker protections, payment in due course), KYC and AML norms, types of accounts and their treatment (including inoperative accounts), asset classification and provisioning under RBI's prudential norms, and digital banking. Questions combine legal concepts with practical scenarios, so focus on applying rules to cases.
questions: In a safe deposit locker facility, the relationship between the bank and the customer is that of:
Debtor and creditor
Trustee and beneficiary
Lessor and lessee
Agent and principal
The bank lets out the locker space to the customer, creating a lessor–lessee relationship. The bank does not know or hold the contents as a debtor would hold deposits.
A customer has given a mandate to her son to operate her account. The mandate is automatically terminated when:
The customer dies
The son changes his job
The account balance falls below ₹10,000
The bank changes the branch manager
A mandate is an agency; it ends on the death, insanity or insolvency of the principal (the customer). Changes in the agent's job or the bank's staff do not end it.
A savings account with no customer-induced transactions for over two years is classified as:
Closed
Inoperative
NPA
Frozen by court order
RBI treats accounts with no customer-induced transactions for more than two years as inoperative (dormant). Balances remain the customer's and can be reactivated after KYC.
A cheque bearing the words 'Not Negotiable' between two parallel lines:
Cannot be transferred to anyone at all
Must be paid in cash at the counter
Can be collected only for a bank's own account
Can be transferred, but the transferee gets no better title than the transferor
'Not negotiable' crossing removes the negotiability feature: the cheque can still be transferred, but a transferee cannot get a better title than the person who transferred it.
A cash credit account is treated as an NPA when it remains 'out of order' for:
More than 90 days
More than 30 days
More than 180 days
More than one year
Under RBI's IRAC norms, an overdraft or cash credit account that is out of order (for example, balance above limit or no credits to cover interest) for over 90 days becomes an NPA.
A loan classified as doubtful (up to one year in that category) has a secured portion of ₹40 lakh and an unsecured portion of ₹10 lakh. The provision required under IRAC norms is:
₹10 lakh
₹20 lakh
₹14 lakh
₹50 lakh
For D1, the unsecured portion needs 100% provision (₹10 lakh) and the secured portion 25% (₹10 lakh), giving ₹20 lakh in total.
Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 'payment in due course' requires payment to be made:
Only to the drawer of the cheque in person
Within one week of the date of the cheque
In cash, irrespective of the crossing
As per the apparent tenor of the instrument, in good faith and without negligence
Payment in due course protects the paying banker when it pays according to the apparent tenor, in good faith, without negligence, to the person in possession entitled to payment.
Which RBI-permitted method allows banks to complete customer identification remotely using a live, consent-based video interaction?
Offline Aadhaar e-sign
NEFT verification
V-CIP
Positive Pay
Video-based Customer Identification Process lets regulated entities verify customers through a secure live video session, with consent, as an alternative to in-person verification.

Accounting & Financial Management for Ba.overview: This paper covers accounting basics and financial calculations bankers use. Revise double entry and the treatment of non-cash items, final accounts, ratio analysis (liquidity, leverage, profitability), working capital, time value of money (simple and compound interest, present value, annuities), depreciation and foreign exchange basics. Many questions are numerical, so practise calculations carefully and check units such as days in a year and compounding periods.
questions: A firm has total debt of ₹60 lakh and shareholders' equity of ₹40 lakh. Its debt–equity ratio is:
Debt–equity = debt / equity = 60 / 40 = 1.5. 0.6 is debt divided by total capital, a different ratio.
Current assets are ₹8 lakh, of which inventory is ₹3 lakh. Current liabilities are ₹4 lakh. The quick ratio is:
Quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) / current liabilities = (8 − 3) / 4 = 1.25. The current ratio would be 2.0.
Simple interest on ₹50,000 at 9% per annum for 146 days (365-day year) is:
SI = 50,000 × 9% × 146 / 365 = ₹1,800. ₹4,500 is interest for a full year.
The present value of ₹1,00,000 receivable after 3 years at 10% compounded annually is closest to:
PV = 1,00,000 / (1.10)^3 = 1,00,000 / 1.331 = ₹75,131. Subtracting 30% simple interest gives ₹70,000, which is wrong.
₹10,000 is deposited at the end of each year for 3 years at 10% compounded annually. The value at the end of year 3 is:
FV = 10,000 × (1.1² + 1.1 + 1) = 10,000 × 3.31 = ₹33,100. ₹36,410 assumes deposits at the start of each year (annuity due).
Why is depreciation added back to net profit when estimating cash generated from operations?
It is a cash receipt from customers
It is a tax refund
It is a non-cash expense
It is a capital receipt
Depreciation reduces profit but involves no cash outflow in the year, so it is added back to profit to arrive at operating cash flow.
Net working capital is defined as:
Current assets minus current liabilities
Fixed assets minus long-term loans
Total assets minus total liabilities
Share capital plus reserves
Net working capital measures short-term liquidity: the excess of current assets over current liabilities that is financed from long-term sources.
A quote 'EUR 1 = ₹95.20' in India is a direct quote. The equivalent indirect quote is about:
An indirect quote states foreign currency per unit of home currency: 1 / 95.20 ≈ 0.0105 EUR per rupee.

Retail Banking & Wealth Management.overview: This paper covers retail banking products, delivery channels and wealth management. Revise retail loan products and appraisal (FOIR, LTV, EMI), credit cards and credit scores, RBI's digital lending and Key Fact Statement norms, payment systems, bancassurance and third-party products, and wealth management basics such as risk profiling, asset allocation and the financial planning process. Practise EMI and eligibility calculations and know the customer-protection rules for retail lending.
questions: A home loan of ₹10 lakh at 9% per annum is repayable in 120 monthly instalments. The EMI is closest to:
EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n / [(1 + r)^n − 1] with r = 0.75% and n = 120, giving about ₹12,668. ₹15,833 assumes flat interest on the full principal.
Under RBI's digital lending guidelines, loan disbursals by regulated entities must generally be made:
Into the lending app's pool account
In cash through agents
Directly into the borrower's bank account
Into the account of the loan service provider
RBI requires disbursals and repayments to flow directly between the borrower's and the lender's accounts, without pass-through or pool accounts of third parties.
A Key Fact Statement (KFS) for retail and MSME loans mainly helps the borrower by:
Guaranteeing loan approval within a day
Removing the need for KYC
Fixing the interest rate for life
Disclosing the all-in cost (APR) and key terms before signing
RBI mandates a KFS in a standard format showing the annual percentage rate, fees and charges and other key terms, so borrowers can compare loans before committing.
A credit card holder pays only the 'minimum amount due' each month. The likely result is:
No interest charged at all
Interest charged on the unpaid balance and loss of the interest-free period
Automatic closure of the card
A higher credit limit the next month
Paying only the minimum avoids a late fee but interest is charged on the outstanding balance, and new purchases lose the interest-free period.
A borrower earns ₹80,000 a month and existing EMIs are ₹12,000. The bank caps total EMIs at 50% of income. The maximum new EMI is:
Allowed EMIs = 50% × 80,000 = ₹40,000. Less existing EMIs of ₹12,000 leaves ₹28,000 for the new loan.
Before recommending investment products to a customer, a bank's wealth manager should first:
Recommend the product with the highest commission
Ask for the customer's net banking password
Sell insurance to cover all risks
Assess the customer's risk profile and goals
Suitability starts with understanding goals, horizon and risk appetite. Commission-led selling causes mis-selling, and passwords must never be asked for.
Credit scores issued by credit information companies in India typically range from:
1 to 10
Most CICs in India use a range of about 300 to 900, where higher scores indicate better credit history and lower risk.
A bank sells mutual fund units to its customers as a distributor. In this role, the bank:
Earns commission and must follow distribution norms
Guarantees the returns of the scheme
Becomes the trustee of the mutual fund
Holds the scheme's securities as custodian
As a distributor the bank earns trail commission and must follow SEBI/AMFI norms, including suitability and disclosure. Returns are not guaranteed by the bank.

Advanced Bank Management.overview: This paper combines statistics, human resource management and credit management for bank managers. Revise measures of central tendency and dispersion (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, coefficient of variation), basic probability, motivation theories (Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor), training and performance appraisal methods, and working capital assessment methods such as MPBF under Tandon Committee norms. Many questions are numerical, so practise short statistical and credit calculations.
questions: The arithmetic mean of 4, 8, 15, 23 and 42 is:
Mean = (4 + 8 + 15 + 23 + 42) / 5 = 92 / 5 = 18.4. The median of the series is 15, a different measure.
A loan portfolio's monthly returns have a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 6. The coefficient of variation is:
CV = standard deviation / mean × 100 = 6 / 40 × 100 = 15%. It expresses relative variability and lets us compare series with different means.
Using Tandon second-method norms, what is the MPBF for a unit whose projected chargeable current assets total ₹500 lakh while creditors and other non-bank current liabilities total ₹200 lakh?
₹175 lakh
₹225 lakh
₹300 lakh
₹125 lakh
Method II: MPBF = 75% of current assets − other current liabilities = 375 − 200 = ₹175 lakh. Method I would give 75% of (500 − 200) = ₹225 lakh.
A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack of 52. The probability that it is a king or a heart is:
P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Adding 4 and 13 without removing the king of hearts double-counts it.
McGregor's Theory Y assumes that employees:
Dislike work and must be closely controlled
Are motivated only by money
Avoid all forms of responsibility
Can be self-directed and seek responsibility
Theory Y holds that people find work natural, can exercise self-control and seek responsibility. Theory X assumes the opposite and favours close supervision.
Job rotation as a training method mainly helps employees to:
Gain exposure to different roles
Avoid performance appraisal
Get a guaranteed promotion
Reduce their working hours
Rotating staff across desks such as credit, forex and operations broadens skills and prepares them for wider responsibilities.
In a series 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 9, 9, 12, the mode is:
The mode is the value that occurs most often. 9 appears three times, more than any other value.
A borrower's 'drawing power' in a cash credit account is mainly determined by:
The borrower's net worth only
Value of current assets less margin
The number of years of banking relationship
The interest rate on the loan
Drawing power is computed from eligible stock and receivables minus the stipulated margin, and limits how much can be drawn within the sanctioned limit.

Bank Financial Management.overview: This paper covers international banking, risk management and balance sheet management. Revise foreign exchange (cross rates, forward premium), trade finance (types of letters of credit, UCP 600), Basel III capital and liquidity norms (CRAR, LCR, NSFR, leverage ratio), interest rate risk measurement (gap and duration gap), and credit risk concepts such as expected loss using PD, LGD and EAD. Numerical questions are common, so practise each formula with simple figures.
questions: A bank has total capital of ₹1,250 crore and risk-weighted assets of ₹10,000 crore. Its CRAR is:
CRAR = capital / RWA × 100 = 1,250 / 10,000 × 100 = 12.5%. This is compared with the regulatory minimum including buffers.
A bank has rate-sensitive assets of ₹800 crore and rate-sensitive liabilities of ₹600 crore. If rates rise by 1%, net interest income will:
Rise by about ₹2 crore
Fall by about ₹2 crore
Rise by about ₹14 crore
Remain unchanged
Gap = RSA − RSL = +₹200 crore (positive gap). A 1% rise increases NII by about 200 × 1% = ₹2 crore.
If GBP/USD is 1.27 and USD/INR is 85.00, the GBP/INR cross rate is:
GBP/INR = GBP/USD × USD/INR = 1.27 × 85.00 = 107.95. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 66.93.
A loan exposure of ₹100 crore has a probability of default of 2% and loss given default of 45%. The expected loss is:
₹2 crore
₹45 crore
₹4.5 crore
₹0.9 crore
Expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD = 0.02 × 0.45 × 100 = ₹0.9 crore. It is covered by pricing and provisions, while unexpected loss is covered by capital.
The Net Stable Funding Ratio under Basel III requires that:
Available stable funding is at least 100% of required stable funding
High-quality liquid assets cover net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period
Tier 1 capital is at least 4% of exposure
Banks hold 4% of deposits as CRR
NSFR ensures a stable funding profile over a one-year horizon. The 30-day stress test is the LCR, and the 4% exposure measure is the leverage ratio.
An exporter receives an LC and uses it as security to have his bank open a second LC in favour of his supplier. The second LC is a:
Revolving LC
Back-to-back LC
Red clause LC
Standby LC
A back-to-back LC is opened on the strength of an export LC, typically for an intermediary who needs to pay a supplier. A red clause LC allows pre-shipment advances.
A bank's assets have a duration of 4 years and its liabilities 2 years, with liabilities at 90% of assets. If rates rise, the bank's equity value will most likely:
Rise
Remain unchanged
Double
Fall
Duration gap = 4 − 0.9 × 2 = 2.2 years (positive). With a positive gap, assets lose more value than liabilities when rates rise, so equity falls.
Under UCP 600, banks examining documents under an LC must determine compliance on the basis of:
Physical inspection of the goods
The buyer's verbal confirmation
The documents alone, on their face
The seller's credit rating
UCP 600 says banks deal with documents, not goods. They check whether documents appear on their face to comply with the credit's terms.

Advanced Business & Financial Management.overview: This paper covers corporate finance, business strategy and the economic environment. Revise capital budgeting (NPV, IRR, payback), cost of capital (CAPM, WACC), leverage (operating and financial), inventory models such as EOQ, valuation and mergers, and strategic tools such as Ansoff's matrix, BCG matrix and Porter's five forces. Practise calculations and know when each tool is applied in decision-making.
questions: A project costs ₹1,00,000 and generates ₹50,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. At a 10% discount rate, its NPV is closest to:
Annual demand is 10,000 units, ordering cost is ₹200 per order and holding cost is ₹4 per unit per year. The economic order quantity is:
500 units
1,000 units
2,000 units
707 units
EOQ = √(2 × D × S / H) = √(2 × 10,000 × 200 / 4) = √10,00,000 = 1,000 units. At EOQ, ordering and holding costs are equal.
The risk-free rate is 7%, the market return is 12% and a share's beta is 1.2. By CAPM, its cost of equity is:
Cost of equity = 7 + 1.2 × (12 − 7) = 7 + 6 = 13%. 14.4% wrongly multiplies the whole market return by beta.
A firm's EBIT is ₹50 crore and interest is ₹10 crore. Its degree of financial leverage is:
DFL = EBIT / (EBIT − interest) = 50 / 40 = 1.25. It shows that a 1% change in EBIT changes EPS by about 1.25%.
The internal rate of return of a project is the discount rate at which:
Payback equals project life
NPV equals zero
Profit is maximum
Cash inflows double
IRR is the rate that makes the present value of inflows equal to the initial outlay, so NPV is zero. Projects with IRR above the cost of capital add value.
In Ansoff's matrix, selling existing products in new markets is called:
Product development
Diversification
Market development
Market penetration
Market development takes current products to new customer segments or geographies. Product development offers new products to existing markets.
A project costs ₹6,00,000 and returns ₹1,50,000 a year for 4 years and ₹2,00,000 in year 5. Its payback period is:
4 years
3 years
5 years
4.5 years
Cumulative inflows reach 1,50,000 × 4 = ₹6,00,000 by the end of year 4, recovering the cost exactly, so payback is 4 years.
Which of the following increases a firm's operating leverage?
Higher interest payments on the firm's borrowed funds
Lower fixed costs
A higher dividend payout
Higher fixed costs relative to variable costs
Operating leverage arises from fixed operating costs. Interest affects financial leverage, not operating leverage.

Banking Regulations & Business Laws.overview: This paper covers the laws that govern banks and their business dealings. Revise key provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and RBI Act (licensing, CRR, SLR, RBI powers over management), recovery laws (SARFAESI, DRT, IBC), the Negotiable Instruments Act for cheque dishonour, the Indian Contract Act (guarantee, indemnity, bailment), consumer protection, and evidence of bank records. Know the purpose of each provision and apply it to practical scenarios.
questions: RBI's power to remove a managerial person or director of a banking company in public interest is under:
Section 36AA of the Banking Regulation Act
Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
Section 13 of SARFAESI Act
Section 138 of the NI Act
Section 36AA empowers RBI to remove chairmen, directors or other managerial personnel of banking companies where necessary in public interest or to protect depositors.
The Cash Reserve Ratio that scheduled banks maintain with RBI is prescribed under:
Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act
Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act
Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934
Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act
CRR is maintained under Section 42 of the RBI Act. SLR, by contrast, is prescribed under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act.
A complaint for dishonour of a cheque under Section 138 of the NI Act must be filed within:
Three months of the cheque date
One year of dishonour
Seven days of the notice
One month of the date the cause of action arises
The cause of action arises when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving notice. The complaint must then be filed within one month, though courts can condone delay.
Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission hears complaints where the value of goods or services paid is up to:
₹1 crore
₹50 lakh
₹10 lakh
₹10 crore
Following the 2021 revision of pecuniary limits, District Commissions handle complaints up to ₹50 lakh; State Commissions handle ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore, and the National Commission above that.
Under SARFAESI, a secured creditor facing resistance in taking possession of secured assets can seek assistance from the:
Civil court of the area
Banking Ombudsman
Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate
Registrar of Companies
Section 14 of SARFAESI allows a secured creditor to request the CMM or DM to take possession of secured assets and documents and hand them over.
A contract of guarantee under the Indian Contract Act involves:
Two parties only: the indemnifier and the indemnity holder, with no third party
Only the creditor and the debtor
Four parties including a trustee
Three parties: creditor, principal debtor and surety
A guarantee has three parties: the creditor, the principal debtor and the surety. A contract of indemnity has two parties.
Under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, entries in a bank's books can be proved in court by:
Producing the original ledger in court in every single case
Certified copies of the entries
Oral evidence of the branch manager only
The customer's passbook alone
The Act allows certified copies of entries in bankers' books to be accepted as prima facie evidence, so banks need not produce original books in court.
A bank wants to start insolvency proceedings against a corporate borrower under the IBC. The application is filed before the:
National Company Law Tribunal
Debts Recovery Tribunal
High Court
District Consumer Commission
Corporate insolvency resolution under the IBC is initiated before the NCLT, which is the adjudicating authority for companies. The DRT handles individual and partnership insolvency.
